2.referenceTitle: Transformation of arsenic species from seafood consumption during in vitro digestion
2.citation: Liu B, Sui J, Feng R, Lin H, Han X, Sun X, Cao L. Transformation of arsenic species from seafood consumption during in vitro digestion. Frontiers in Nutrition. 2023;10:1207732. Published 12 October 2023. doi:10.3389/fnut.2023.1207732.
2.summary: Cooked crab, scallop, turbot and flounder underwent simulated digestion. HPLC-ICP-MS showed approximately two- to three-fold increases in As(V) amounts for crab and scallop, while inorganic arsenic was undetected in digested fish. Separate standards experiments explored conversion under acidic conditions.
2.establishes: The results demonstrate changes within this laboratory protocol. They do not measure absorption, human body burden or clinical toxicity. The proposed radical mechanism and pH effects cannot establish the fraction converted inside a living person.
2.relevance: HMTc can use this to explain why food speciation and absorbed dose are distinct. It does not establish a new numeric ceiling or certify the safety of all organic arsenic compounds.

3.referenceTitle: Elevated arsenic level in fasting serum via ingestion of fish meat increased the risk of hypertension in humans and mice
3.citation: Kagawa T, Ohgami N, He T, et al. Elevated arsenic level in fasting serum via ingestion of fish meat increased the risk of hypertension in humans and mice. European Heart Journal Open. 2023;3(5):oead074. Published 4 September 2023. doi:10.1093/ehjopen/oead074.
3.summary: Among 2,709 Japanese adults aged 39–75, this cross-sectional analysis associated fasting serum total arsenic with hypertension prevalence. A separate mouse experiment administered a mixture containing inorganic arsenic, DMA, arsenobetaine and trimethylarsine oxide.
3.establishes: Human serum arsenic was not speciated. The design cannot establish temporal causation or attribute the association to arsenobetaine; the animal mixture also cannot isolate one species.
3.relevance: For HMTc, the study motivates species-specific research but supplies no product threshold or evidence that an inorganic-arsenic-only limit resolves every organic-arsenic uncertainty.

4.referenceTitle: First detection of an arsenosugar phospholipid in the microalga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii
4.citation: Raab A, Zhang J, Ge Y, Fernández-Mendoza F, Feldmann J. Lipophilic arsenic compounds in the cultured green alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii. Analytical and Bioanalytical Chemistry. 2024;416:2809–2818. Published 8 January 2024. doi:10.1007/s00216-023-05122-7.
4.summary: Laboratory-grown C. reinhardtii exposed to 20 µg/L arsenate for seven days contained about 57% of its arsenic as arsenolipids. Fractionation and mass spectrometry identified abundant arsenoriboside-containing phytols and compared the profile with wild Saccharina latissima.
4.establishes: This characterizes an exposed freshwater model organism. It does not measure commercial spirulina, chlorella or algae oils, establish human toxicity, or demonstrate failure of routine total-arsenic digestion.
4.relevance: For HMTc, it supports checking whether a method characterizes the intended chemical fraction in a particular ingredient. Commercial-product assumptions require separate data.

5.referenceTitle: Arsenobetaine amide: a novel arsenic species detected in several mushroom species
5.citation: Walenta M, Raab A, Braeuer S, Steiner L, Borovička J, Goessler W. Arsenobetaine amide: a novel arsenic species detected in several mushroom species. Analytical and Bioanalytical Chemistry. 2024;416:1399–1405. Published 16 January 2024. doi:10.1007/s00216-024-05132-z.
5.summary: The authors examined eleven selected mushroom fruiting-body collections representing four species from Austria and the Czech Republic. They isolated arsenobetaine amide, confirmed its identity using synthesis and analytical comparison, and reported 0.15–9.6% of total arsenic in the studied samples.
5.establishes: This discovery establishes chemical diversity in selected fungi, including collections from contaminated regions. It is not a representative edible-mushroom survey or a toxicological test of arsenobetaine amide.
5.relevance: HMTc can use it to explain why unidentified organic species should remain explicit analytical uncertainties. Neither arsenobetaine toxicity nor a numerical food limit follows from identifying a related compound.

6.referenceTitle: Inorganic arsenic in seaweed: a fast HPLC-ICP-MS method without coelution of arsenosugars
6.citation: Sim R, Weyer M, Pétursdóttir ÁH. Inorganic arsenic in seaweed: a fast HPLC-ICP-MS method without coelution of arsenosugars. Analytical and Bioanalytical Chemistry. 2024;416:3033–3044. Published 23 March 2024. doi:10.1007/s00216-024-05250-8.
6.summary: This single-laboratory validation developed acid/peroxide extraction and chromatographic separation for inorganic arsenic. Certified hijiki recovery was 99 ± 9%. Tested L. digitata meristem and reproductive tissue contained 2.6 and 54 mg/kg inorganic arsenic, with total arsenic of 130 and 210 mg/kg.
6.establishes: The tested dried tissues therefore differed substantially. The method measures inorganic species together after oxidation; it does not fully characterize all arsenicals, and DMA quantification has stated limitations.
6.relevance: For HMTc, it supports matrix-specific validation and selecting the sampled tissue. It does not establish that every Laminaria product contains predominantly inorganic arsenic.

7.referenceTitle: Maximum levels for inorganic arsenic in seaweed and other foods
7.citation: European Commission. Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 of 25 April 2023 on maximum levels for certain contaminants in food and repealing Regulation (EC) No 1881/2006. OJ L119, 5 May 2023, pp. 103–157; entered into force 25 May 2023. Original text and consolidation dated 19 August 2026.
7.summary: The regulation sets binding arsenic maxima for specified food categories. The original inorganic-arsenic section covers rice products, certain infant foods and juices. 7.establishes: Neither reviewed version lists a seaweed-specific inorganic-arsenic maximum in Annex I section 3.4. The existence of arsenic limits for other foods does not create a generic seaweed limit or establish that organic arsenic is harmless.
7.relevance: HMTc must identify the actual jurisdiction, instrument and product category supporting any seaweed ceiling. Its policy of choosing the strictest regulator is separate from what this EU instrument requires.

8.referenceTitle: Heavy Metal Index — the organoarsenical inertness assumption (synthesis with full anchor-source records)
8.citation: Pendergrass K. The organoarsenical inertness assumption. Heavy Metal Index. Updated 13 May 2026. Preprint synthesis. doi:10.83376/hmi.organoarsenical-inertness-assumption.
8.summary: The synthesis combines biomonitoring, simulated-digestion, epidemiological and analytical papers to argue that organic arsenic needs species-specific interpretation. It acknowledges gaps in human absorption evidence and commercial-algae characterization.
8.establishes: The page labels itself a preprint with no external reviews. It is an interpretive synthesis, not a new experiment or an independent validation of the linked records.
8.relevance: It explains the narrative used by HMTc. Shared authorship and Institute of Contaminant Standards affiliation mean it should not serve as independent corroboration or proof of certification efficacy.

1.referenceTitle: High spatial and temporal variation in biomass composition of the novel aquaculture target Ecklonia radiata
1.citation: Nepper-Davidsen J, Glasson CRK, Lawton RJ, Magnusson M. Journal of Applied Phycology. 2023;35:1755–1768. Published 28 April 2023. doi:10.1007/s10811-023-02969-2.
1.summary: The researchers collected wild Ecklonia radiata at 12 North Island sites and monthly at one site in 2019–2020. Metals were measured by ICP-MS in pooled samples. Spatial means were total arsenic 49 mg/kg and cadmium 1.2 mg/kg dry weight.
1.establishes: This characterizes harvested kelp, not finished retail products. Inorganic arsenic was estimated using a literature-based 1% assumption, not measured. The study cannot establish an invariant inorganic fraction or isolate natural from anthropogenic contamination.
1.relevance: It supports batch- and species-specific measurements. The page’s 2.45 µg serving calculation is hypothetical arithmetic, not an observed inorganic-arsenic dose.

2.referenceTitle: Chemical contaminant levels in edible seaweeds of the Salish Sea and implications for their consumption
2.citation: Hahn JL, Van Alstyne KL, Gaydos JK, et al. PLOS ONE. 2022;17(9):e0269269. Published 23 September 2022. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0269269.
2.summary: Three brown-seaweed species were collected across 43 Salish Sea sites in summer 2015 and analyzed for metals by ICP-MS. Bull kelp averaged 5.69 mg/kg cadmium dry weight. Sites deliberately included locations with known or suspected contamination.
2.establishes: Arsenic was not speciated. Cadmium exceeded selected international recommendations but remained below the authors’ US dose-based screening level and their moisture-adjusted EU comparison. These comparisons do not establish universal legal noncompliance.
2.relevance: The study supports location- and species-specific screening; it cannot establish that sourcing is ineffective or that pollution is irrelevant.

3.referenceTitle: EFSA scientific opinion on heavy metals and iodine in seaweeds and halophytes as food
3.citation: EFSA, Dujardin B, Ferreira de Sousa R, Gómez Ruiz JA. Dietary exposure to heavy metals and iodine intake via consumption of seaweeds and halophytes in the European population. EFSA Journal. 2023;21(1):7798. doi:10.2903/j.efsa.2023.7798.
3.summary: This exposure report combined 2011–2021 occurrence data, including 2,093 cadmium and 920 inorganic-arsenic results, with consumption records for 468 people. Seaweed consumption could contribute materially to exposure, with substantial differences among products and species.
3.establishes: It is an EFSA scientific report, endorsed by CONTAM, not a new contaminant-limit regulation. Sparse consumption records, food coding, processing and sample representativeness constrain estimates. It identifies unresolved organic-arsenic toxicology as well as inorganic-arsenic concerns.
3.relevance: It supports speciation and product-specific exposure assessment, while neither prescribing HMTc ceilings nor validating a certification program.

4.referenceTitle: Maximum levels for contaminants in food
4.citation: European Commission. Regulation (EU) 2023/915 of 25 April 2023. OJ L 119, 5 May 2023, pp. 103–157; effective 25 May 2023. Original act and consolidated text dated 19 August 2026.
4.summary: The regulation sets category-specific food maxima. Cadmium is limited to 3 mg/kg in supplements containing at least 80% dried seaweed, seaweed-derived products or dried bivalves; other supplements have a 1 mg/kg limit. The reviewed text has no general whole-seaweed cadmium or inorganic-arsenic row.
4.establishes: Articles 2–3 govern market placement, edible portions and processing factors. Supplement limits cannot be transferred automatically to whole seaweed, snacks, or animal feed. A scientific exposure report does not itself create a maximum.
4.relevance: It supplies legal category benchmarks; selecting stricter occurrence-based HMTc limits remains a program decision, not a rule imposed by this regulation.

5.referenceTitle: US FDA Closer to Zero action plan and inorganic-arsenic guidance
5.citation: US FDA. Closer to Zero action plan, launched April 2021; Inorganic Arsenic in Rice Cereals for Infants: Action Level, final guidance August 2020; FDA arsenic/cadmium regulatory-information pages.
5.summary: Closer to Zero prioritizes foods consumed by babies and young children. The rice-cereal guidance recommends an inorganic-arsenic action level of 100 µg/kg. It is nonbinding guidance for infant rice cereal, not a seaweed standard.
5.establishes: These documents do not set a seaweed-specific cadmium or arsenic maximum. Their limited scope cannot prove the absence of every federal control; FDA expressly retains authority to act when contaminated food is unsafe.
5.relevance: The sources distinguish a published numerical action level from broader food-safety enforcement. They do not establish that Proposition 65 is the sole or dominant US control.

6.referenceTitle: California Proposition 65 exposure warnings for cadmium and arsenic
6.citation: California OEHHA. Proposition 65 safe-harbor information and Title27 regulations compilation, April 2025; §§ 25501, 25709 and 25805.
6.summary: Proposition 65 uses exposure-based warning rules rather than a universal seaweed concentration maximum. The reviewed regulations give an inorganic-arsenic cancer safe harbor of 10 µg/day except inhalation; OEHHA lists an oral cadmium reproductive-toxicity safe harbor of 4.1 µg/day.
6.establishes: Exceeding a safe harbor is not automatically a product violation. Scientifically valid alternative exposure levels and particular settlements can matter. The naturally occurring-food provision has evidentiary and good-practice conditions; natural origin is not an automatic exemption.
6.relevance: This supports distinguishing warning exposure from food maxima. It does not quantify seaweed enforcement or establish Proposition 65 as the main US regulatory pressure.

7.referenceTitle: Heavy Metal Index — seaweed as a cadmium and arsenic pathway (synthesis with full anchor-source records)
7.citation: Pendergrass K. Heavy Metal Index: seaweed cadmium/arsenic pathway synthesis. Last updated 16 May 2026. Page snapshot identifier 10.83376/hmi.seaweed-cd-as-contamination. Preprint; no external reviews listed at access.
7.summary: This narrative synthesis connects the New Zealand field survey, Salish Sea study and EFSA exposure report. It argues for cadmium and inorganic-arsenic testing and acknowledges that its anchors do not provide a representative US commercial-retail survey.
7.establishes: The synthesis adds interpretation, not an independent occurrence dataset. Its displayed review status is provisional. Author affiliation and the footer identify Institute of Contaminant Standards and Paleo Certified, Inc.; institutional independence is not established.
7.relevance: It explains the article’s interpretive framework. Its source links must be assessed individually before using its causal, regulatory or certification conclusions.

1.referenceTitle: The quality and safety of Rhodiola rosea supplements on the U.S. market: An analysis of biomarkers, heavy metals, and pesticide residues
1.citation: Porwollik S, Jafari M. PLOS One. 2026;21(1):e0341070. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0341070.
1.summary: Ten Rhodiola products bought from Amazon in 2024 were tested: seven capsules and three tinctures. All capsules contained measurable arsenic, cobalt and lead; the tinctures were below the reported analytical thresholds.
1.establishes: Capsule total arsenic ranged from 21–393 ppb and lead from 9–88 ppb; cobalt reached 733 ppb. Total arsenic was not speciated. The 500 mg serving estimate is product-specific. Below detection does not mean metal-free or universally “clean.”
1.relevance: It supports a variable, measurable metal burden in this small product sample. It does not establish contamination prevalence across supplements, prove environmental uptake as the source, or rank supplement enforcement against food enforcement.

2.referenceTitle: Comparison of Regulations for Arsenic and Heavy Metals in Herbal Medicines Using Pharmacopoeias of Nine Counties/Regions
2.citation: Inada I, Kiuchi F, Urushihara H. Therapeutic Innovation & Regulatory Science. 2023;57(5):963–974. doi:10.1007/s43441-023-00532-2; associated correction doi:10.1007/s43441-023-00539-9. Supplementary US context: 21 CFR 111.70 (2025 edition) and FDA Import Alert 99-42 (August 26, 2026).
2.summary: The study compared editions current in December 2021 for Brazil, China, Europe, Hong Kong, India, Japan, Korea, the US and Vietnam, plus WHO and ISO documents. Limits, analytical methods and monograph coverage differed.
2.establishes: The article’s Taiwan/Britain list is incorrect. The Indian document was Indian Pharmacopoeia 2018; the Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia was expressly excluded. WHO values were not a universally followed floor. The study compared written standards, not enforcement intensity or certification outcomes.

3.referenceTitle: Lead poisoning from Ayurvedic treatment: a further case.
3.citation: Ciocan C, Mansour I, Beneduce A, et al. La Medicina del Lavoro. 2021;112(2):162–167. doi:10.23749/mdl.v112i2.10576.
3.summary: An Indian sailor treated in Italy had blood lead reported at 102 µg/dL after Ayurvedic medicine use. Testing two preparations, including three mixtures of one preparation, found lead up to 23,043.02 mg/kg and mercury up to 145,710.64 mg/kg. He received three chelation cycles.

No product mercury speciation was performed; poor inorganic-mercury absorption was offered as a possible explanation, not established causation.
3.relevance: It supports the existence of extremely contaminated preparations and the need to investigate product exposure. It does not prove intentional addition in every product, sulphide identity, universal absence of food analogues, or that testing is the only possible preventive measure.

4.citation: Thomas J, Sebastian R, Anil Kumar CR, Rafi AM. Endocrinology, Diabetes & Metabolism Case Reports. 2024;2024(2):23-0066. doi:10.1530/EDM-23-0066.
4.summary: A 58-year-old woman in Kerala developed lead poisoning after about 1.5 months taking an internet-purchased herbal diabetes product. Blood lead was 121.20 µg/dL; the reported state drug-analyst result for the capsule was approximately 40,657 ppm lead.

1.referenceTitle: Taiwan FDA amended analytical method

2.citation: U.S. Food and Drug Administration. FDA’s Infant Formula Product Testing Results. 2026 release reporting the FY2023–2025 market-basket survey; accessed September 15, 2026.

3.referenceTitle: EPA Lead and Copper Rule Improvements
3.citation: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Lead and Copper Rule Improvements; official rule hub and October 2024 general fact sheet. Final rule:89 FR 86418, October 30, 2024, effective December 30, 2024.

4.citation: European Commission. Packaging waste: overview of Regulation (EU) 2025/40 on packaging and packaging waste. Regulation adopted December 19, 2024; entered into force February 11, 2025; generally applies August 12, 2026.

The linked regulation separately addresses substances of concern, technical documentation and packaging composition; Article 5(4) sets a combined 100 mg/kg ceiling for lead, cadmium, mercury and hexavalent chromium in packaging or components.
4.establishes: This is a packaging-composition rule, not a food or migration limit. General application does not mean every design requirement starts simultaneously, and preserved decisions and derogations require separate checks.
4.relevance: It supports a distinct packaging evidence record alongside HMTc food results. Food testing alone cannot demonstrate packaging composition or satisfy its technical documentation.

5.citation: European Parliament and Council. Regulation (EU) 2024/1849 of June 13, 2024 amending Regulation (EU) 2017/852 on mercury regarding dental amalgam and other mercury-added products. OJ L2024/1849, July 10, 2024.

5.establishes: The temporary qualifying Member-State use derogation ended June 30, 2026; specific medical exceptions remain. The lamp restrictions concern listed products and activities, not all mercury-containing objects or food concentrations.
5.relevance: This illustrates why HMTc’s regulatory register must distinguish product bans and their timetables from food thresholds. The regulation does not independently create a duty for every food brand.

6.citation: Health Canada. Modification to the Lists of Permitted Food Additives to revise certain permitted uses of aluminum-containing food additives. Notice M-FAA-25-03, September 15, 2025.
6.summary: The notice announces revised or removed additive permissions, generally effective October 20, 2025. Removal of potassium aluminum sulphate as a firming agent in pickles and relishes is delayed until January 1, 2028.
6.establishes: The changes concern authorized uses and use levels. They are not a new across-food aluminum contaminant limit or a blanket additive ban; several uses were retained, and Health Canada reported no identified concern with expected dietary exposure.
6.relevance: The article correctly treats this as a formulation and authorization issue. HMTc evidence should preserve additive identity, function, food category and the relevant transition date separately from contamination testing.

7.referenceTitle: Heavy Metal Index — regulations
7.citation: Pendergrass, K. Regulations. Heavy Metal Index, Institute of Contaminant Standards. Directory page displaying last updated May 3, 2026; accessed September 15, 2026.
7.summary: This publisher-maintained directory organizes regulatory thresholds, action levels and guidance by jurisdiction and topic, with links to instrument pages and comparison views.

1.referenceTitle: Meta-analysis of public health risks of lead accumulation in wastewater, irrigated soil, and crops nexus
1.citation: Ali, Adane Sirage; Bayih, Argaw Ambelu; and Gari, Sirak Robele. Meta-analysis of public health risks of lead accumulation in wastewater, irrigated soil, and crops nexus. Frontiers in Public Health 10:977721, 18 October 2022. doi:10.3389/fpubh.2022.977721.
1.summary: This review included 24 studies of lead in irrigation wastewater, soils and crops. It reported frequent exceedances of the authors’ selected benchmarks, with substantial differences across settings.
1.establishes: Between-study heterogeneity was very high (I²=98%). The review concerns lead, not a pooled multi-metal effect; its modeled risk indices are not observations of illness or proof of a particular causal source.
1.relevance: It supports screening wastewater-linked supply chains for lead. It does not verify current WHO/FAO legal limits, a uniform effect size, or the article’s broader claim that several metals always rise together.

2.referenceTitle: Levels of heavy metals and their health risk assessment from wastewater irrigated spinach in railway quarters, Bauchi, Bauchi state, Nigeria
2.citation: Adebayo RK, Hassan UF, Adamu HM, Hassan HF, Baba H, Ajiya DA. Levels of heavy metals and their health risk assessment from wastewater irrigated spinach in railway quarters, Bauchi, Bauchi state, Nigeria. International Journal of Advanced Chemistry Research 2(2):12–17, 21 July 2020. doi:10.33545/26646781.2020.v2.i2a.22.
2.summary: The authors analyzed irrigation water and dried edible African spinach from one Bauchi farm. Reported spinach concentrations included lead 6.60, cadmium 1.00 and nickel 7.70 mg/kg.
2.establishes: This is a limited site observation, without a matched irrigation control or chromium speciation. Lead exceeded the authors’ selected plant benchmark, while their calculated health-risk indices were below one; neither establishes observed clinical effects or universal safety.
2.relevance: It illustrates several metals in one crop from a wastewater-irrigated farm. HMTc should retain the dried basis and uncertain sample/composite design; a matched control would be needed to demonstrate how much irrigation elevated each metal.

3.referenceTitle: Assessment of Heavy Metal Accumulation in Wastewater–Receiving Soil–Exotic and Indigenous Vegetable Systems and Its Potential Health Risks: A Case Study from Blantyre, Malawi
3.citation: Chiutula C, Mtewa AG, Abraham A, Mvula RLS, Maluwa A, Eregno FE, Njalam’mano J. Assessment of Heavy Metal Accumulation in Wastewater–Receiving Soil–Exotic and Indigenous Vegetable Systems and Its Potential Health Risks: A Case Study from Blantyre, Malawi. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health 22(11):1614, 23 October 2025. doi:10.3390/ijerph22111614.
3.summary: This Soche wastewater-treatment-plant field study measured five metals in water, soil and six vegetable species. Water samples had nondetectable cadmium, chromium and lead, while vegetable results varied by species and tissue.
3.establishes: The sampling provides a snapshot, not a measured history of decades of loading. The study used dried plant material and total-element analysis; its unit reporting and food-limit comparisons require care. It did not establish Cr(VI) concentrations.
3.relevance: It supports measuring crops as well as water. The article’s definite attribution to historical soil loading remains an interpretation; unit inconsistencies and exposure-model assumptions prevent adopting every stated exceedance as a verified food-law breach.

4.referenceTitle: Uptake of Arsenic by Irrigated Vegetables and Cooked Food Products in Burkina Faso
4.citation: Clair-Caliot G, Marks SJ, Hug SJ, Bretzler A, N’guessan ND, Tihe SFK, Lalanne F. Uptake of Arsenic by Irrigated Vegetables and Cooked Food Products in Burkina Faso. Frontiers in Water 3:667308, 26 July 2021. doi:10.3389/frwa.2021.667308.
4.summary: A greenhouse experiment grew seven vegetables in 168 pots with arsenate-spiked irrigation water at 0–1,000 µg/L. Average dry-mass arsenic was higher in leafy edible parts than roots or fruits; cooking-water contamination also changed food arsenic.
4.establishes: The experiment models geogenic groundwater, not municipal sewage or retail prevalence. Species differed, and incomplete organ sampling limits some transfer comparisons. Its health indices use exposure assumptions rather than measured illness.
4.relevance: It supports considering crop type and water quality. HMTc cannot generalize this arsenic-specific controlled experiment into proof that wastewater raises every metal or that one crop hierarchy applies across all contaminants.

5.referenceTitle: HEAVY METALS IN SOIL AND VEGETABLES AND THEIR EFFECT ON HEALTH
5.citation: Pal J, Bishnoi M, Kaur M. Heavy metals in soil and vegetables and their effect on health. International Journal of Engineering Science Technologies 2(1):17–27, September 2017. doi:10.29121/IJOEST.v2.i1.2017.03.
5.summary: This Hisar field survey measured six metals in six vegetables and environmental samples from three wastewater-irrigated locations. Uptake varied by vegetable, element and location; cadmium and nickel transfer were relatively high in spinach.
5.establishes: Dried samples and atomic absorption establish total-element concentrations, not chromium species. The authors’ modeled health indices were below one, but their reference values and limited exposure pathways do not establish universal safety or observed disease.
5.relevance: It supports retaining crop-specific measurements within broader panels. It does not prove that leafy vegetables always rank highest for every metal, or validate HMTc’s thresholds and testing frequency.

7.referenceTitle: Heavy Metal Index — wastewater-irrigation multi-metal crop pathway (synthesis with full anchor-source records)
7.citation: Pendergrass, Karen. Wastewater and sewage-effluent irrigation is a single upstream pathway that co-elevates multiple metals in the same crop, concentrating in leafy greens on peri-urban plots across the Global South. Heavy Metal Index, updated 27 July 2026. Preprint synthesis; doi:10.83376/hmi.wastewater-irrigation-multimetal-crop-pathway.
7.summary: The synthesis connects five sources on irrigation-related crop contamination, including a lead meta-analysis, field surveys and a controlled arsenic-irrigation experiment.
7.establishes: It is an author’s interpretation, with no external review recorded on the examined page. The arsenic experiment models geogenic groundwater rather than sewage, and the evidence does not uniformly isolate irrigation from other inputs.
7.relevance: It maps the studies behind this article’s broader testing argument. HMTc’s panel and surveillance schedule remain program decisions; a separate Index page with shared authorship is not independent corroboration.

1.referenceTitle: Hain Celestial Group, Inc. v. Palmquist
1.citation: Supreme Court of the United States. Hain Celestial Group, Inc. v. Palmquist, No. 24-724, 607 U.S. ___ (2026), unanimous opinion by Justice Sotomayor, 24 February 2026.
1.summary: The Court affirmed that erroneous dismissal of a retailer whose citizenship defeated federal diversity jurisdiction did not cure the jurisdictional defect. The manufacturer’s favorable federal judgment therefore could not stand.
1.establishes: This procedural holding does not decide injury causation, product defects or certification. Properly curing a jurisdictional defect remains different from wrongly dismissing a party; the decision does not prohibit all retailer dismissals or require a jury trial after every remand.
1.relevance: It supplies the legal event behind this briefing’s emphasis on records that can be examined in different courts. Predictions about widespread state-court trials, greater settlement pressure and certification’s economic value are the author’s analysis, not court findings.

2.referenceTitle: Palmquist v. Hain Celestial Group, Inc.
2.citation: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit. Palmquist v. Hain Celestial Group, Inc., No. 23-40197, opinion by Judge Carl E. Stewart, 28 May 2024.
2.summary: The Fifth Circuit found that the pleaded claims against Whole Foods supported remand, vacated the federal judgment and directed return to state court. Its factual background also describes Hain’s testing history.
2.establishes: The federal win was judgment as a matter of law under Rule 50 after the plaintiffs rested, not a defense jury verdict. The appellate court resolved jurisdiction and expressly did not decide whether the merits judgment was correct.
2.relevance: It explains the procedural cost of litigating in a court without jurisdiction. Its account of Hain beginning finished-product testing in 2019 provides context for the briefing’s recordkeeping argument, but does not establish that a testing narrative replaces proof of causation.

3.referenceTitle: Baby Foods Are Tainted with Dangerous Levels of Arsenic, Lead, Cadmium, and Mercury
3.citation: U.S. House of Representatives, Committee on Oversight and Reform, Subcommittee on Economic and Consumer Policy. Baby Foods Are Tainted with Dangerous Levels of Arsenic, Lead, Cadmium, and Mercury. Staff report, 4 February 2021.
3.summary: Congressional staff reviewed manufacturers’ internal documents, identified testing concerns and recommended mandatory finished-product testing. Its Hain discussion describes an August 2019 presentation comparing finished rice foods with estimates based on ingredients.
3.establishes: The report gives staff findings and recommendations, not a court’s liability determination. It does not independently establish the first-ever date of Hain’s finished-product testing or prove that any detectable quantity caused a particular child’s injury.
3.relevance: It explains why the briefing emphasizes routine finished-product evidence. The specific 2019 start date is recited separately in the Fifth Circuit opinion at reference 2; the report itself does not establish litigation outcomes or HMTc effectiveness.

5.referenceTitle: The Counterproductive Consequences of Public Exposé Testing: How Unstructured Disclosure Undermines Heavy Metal Contamination Reduction
5.citation: Pendergrass, Karen. The Counterproductive Consequences of Public Exposé Testing: How Unstructured Disclosure Undermines Heavy Metal Contamination Reduction. Journal of Food Metallomics, preprint, 8 April 2026. doi: 10.5281/zenodo.19470572.
5.summary: This preprint argues that public testing disclosures can generate litigation and discourage brands from joining improvement programs. Section V uses the Amazon rice lawsuit, baby-food litigation and a Proposition 65 settlement as examples.
5.establishes: It is the program architect’s argument, explicitly not yet peer reviewed, rather than an original study of lawsuits or contamination outcomes. Its account of plaintiffs’ theories does not establish scientific causation or a universal rule that any detectable metal causes injury.
5.relevance: It supplies the rationale for HMTc’s confidential remediation proposal. That rationale requires separation from legal privilege and demonstrated benefit: the paper does not show that confidentiality prevents discovery or that certification reduces claims.

6.referenceTitle: California Assembly Bill 899
6.citation: California Assembly Bill 899, Chapter 668, Statutes of 2023, adding California Health and Safety Code §§110962–110963.
6.summary: AB 899 requires testing of specified baby foods for arsenic, cadmium, lead and mercury, followed by public disclosure of results. The enacted law phases testing in from January 2024 and disclosure from January 2025.
6.establishes: These statutory duties concern defined foods for children under two and exclude infant formula. Testing, disclosure and applicable QR labeling are legal obligations within that scope; participation in HMTc is not required.
6.relevance: It supports the briefing’s account of a more demanding documentation environment. HMTc may help organize testing records, but its own surveillance schedule and confidentiality arrangements cannot replace required public disclosure or statutory testing.

7.referenceTitle: Action Levels for Lead in Food Intended for Babies and Young Children: Guidance for Industry
7.citation: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Human Foods Program. Action Levels for Lead in Processed Food Intended for Babies and Young Children: Guidance for Industry. January 2025.
7.summary: FDA recommends lead action levels of 10 or 20 ppb for specified categories of packaged processed foods intended for children under two. The guidance explains exposure, achievability and enforcement considerations.
7.establishes: These are nonbinding action levels that inform case-by-case adulteration and enforcement decisions under existing law, not a safe-exposure guarantee or universal limit for all children’s foods. Formula, beverages and snacks are excluded from this guidance.
7.relevance: It supplies the published regulatory benchmark behind the briefing’s call for interpretable results. HMTc’s selected limits and decision rules remain program choices and do not create a liability safe harbor.

Promix Nutrition, Inc., out-of-court settlement. The bibliography’s People v. Promix Nutrition consent-judgment identification was not verified.

9.referenceTitle: Amazon.com Sued Over Alleged Sale of Contaminated Rice
9.citation: Stempel, Jonathan. Amazon.com is sued over alleged sale of contaminated rice. Reuters, 23 May 2025, syndicated by Investing.com. Primary filing: Wright and Blum v. Amazon.com, Inc., No. 2:25-cv-00977 (W.D. Wash.), class action complaint, ECF No. 1, filed 23 May 2025.
9.summary: Reuters reported a proposed consumer class action alleging that Amazon omitted information about heavy metals in rice products. The matching complaint invokes Washington consumer-protection and fraudulent-concealment theories and cites published third-party testing.
9.establishes: The report and complaint establish the filing and allegations, not contamination findings, class certification or Amazon’s liability. The complaint requests relief; it does not impose a testing obligation or prove that a particular consumer’s purchase caused injury.
9.relevance: This is a concrete example of public testing being used in a marketplace lawsuit, extending the briefing’s discussion beyond baby-food manufacturers. It does not show that HMTc would prevent the claim or establish a universal marketplace certification mandate.

10.referenceTitle: HMTc Infant and Child Foods Program Manual
10.citation: Pendergrass, Karen. Heavy Metal Tested & Certified (HMTc) Infant and Child Foods Program Manual. 2026 edition, v0. The Paleo Foundation, 18 May 2026. doi:10.5281/zenodo.20270512. This is the cited first deposit; later editions supersede it.
10.summary: The cited manual describes staged certification, scheduled testing, data requirements, measurement decision rules, confidential remediation and a process for tightening limits. Its introductory business case repeats the operator’s illustrative loss models.
10.establishes: These are the operator’s specifications and arguments, not evidence of implementation, legal admissibility or reduced litigation. The cited v0 is superseded; it expressly acknowledges subpoena and privilege limits and permits direct comparison with the limit when measurement uncertainty is unreported.
10.relevance: It is the primary source for the program proposed as the briefing’s response to Palmquist. Current rules and agreements must be checked separately; a program-valid record, confidentiality clause or passing result does not by itself determine courtroom admissibility or liability.

11.referenceTitle: Litigation Cost Survey of Major Companies
11.citation: Lawyers for Civil Justice, Civil Justice Reform Group and U.S. Chamber Institute for Legal Reform. Litigation Cost Survey of Major Companies, May 2010. Survey administered by the Searle Center; submitted to the 2010 Conference on Civil Litigation.
11.summary: This industry-sponsored survey reports major companies’ historical litigation costs, including 2008 company means of approximately $2.02 million in outside fees and $622,000 in discovery costs for major cases.
11.establishes: The survey was published in May 2010, not authored by the Federal Judicial Center in 2008. Its selected large-company sample and case threshold limit generalization; mean discovery cost is not evidence of how frequently costs exceed $600,000.
11.relevance: It supplies a historical expense benchmark for the briefing’s business case. It does not measure costs after Palmquist, state-versus-federal differences, or savings from HMTc testing and certification.

12.referenceTitle: ISO/IEC 17025:2017, General Requirements for the Competence of Testing and Calibration Laboratories
12.citation: International Organization for Standardization and International Electrotechnical Commission. ISO/IEC 17025:2017, General requirements for the competence of testing and calibration laboratories. Third edition, November 2017; confirmed in 2023.
12.summary: ISO/IEC 17025 provides a general benchmark for laboratory competence, impartiality and consistent operation. Its official public overview describes testing and calibration laboratories and the role of accreditation.
12.establishes: Only the official overview was reviewed, not the paid normative standard or a particular laboratory’s accreditation. Accreditation does not itself certify a food, prescribe HMTc’s sampling cadence, or guarantee acceptance of evidence in court.
12.relevance: It supports the laboratory-competence requirement in the briefing’s independent-testing proposal. The sampling independence, custody consequences and continuing surveillance described here come from HMTc’s own program rules.

13.referenceTitle: Use of Uncertainty Information in Compliance Assessment
13.citation: Williams, A., and Magnusson, B., editors. Eurachem/CITAC Guide: Use of uncertainty information in compliance assessment. Second edition, 2021. ISBN 978-0-948926-38-9. International Laboratory Accreditation Cooperation. Guidelines on Decision Rules and Statements of Conformity, ILAC-G8:09/2019.
13.summary: These two guides explain how a measured result, its uncertainty and a specification limit can be combined in a documented conformity decision. They describe guard bands, which place acceptance boundaries away from the limit, and conditional or inconclusive outcomes.
13.establishes: They provide analytical guidance, not rules of evidence or a universal HMTc formula. ILAC illustrates a nonbinary rule using expanded uncertainty, while both guides allow different rules suited to the application and acceptable decision risk.
13.relevance: They support the measurement logic behind HMTc’s pass/fail/borderline scheme. HMTc’s exact rule and confirmatory process are program choices; following the guides does not itself establish legal admissibility, safety or a successful defense.

14.referenceTitle: The Cost of Operating Without Credible Third-Party Heavy-Metal Certification
14.citation: Pendergrass, Karen. The Cost of Operating Without Credible Third-Party Heavy-Metal Certification. Journal of Food Metallomics, preprint, 7 March 2026, pp. 1–6. doi: 10.5281/zenodo.18903738.
14.summary: The preprint models one-year losses following a public heavy-metals event and compares expected losses with certification costs. Its mid-size example assumes a $15 million event loss, 3% annual event probability and 25% reduction through certification.
14.establishes: Multiplying those assumptions gives $112,500 annual break-even. The paper does not measure HMTc’s effect on event probability, loss severity or insurance premiums; the assumed reduction and scenario totals are not guarantees.
14.relevance: It supplies the briefing’s break-even calculation. Claims that carriers are repricing in real time or that certified suppliers consistently pay less require insurer-specific evidence beyond this model.

1.referenceTitle: 9 CFR 412.1 — Label approval
1.citation: 9 CFR §412.1, Label approval, January 1, 2025 annual edition, pp 551–552, including adjacent §412.2. USDA, Submission for OMB Review; Comment Request, 91 FR 10582, March 4, 2026, corroborates the generic-approval exception.
1.summary: Section 412.1 requires submission for specified labels, including special claims, while expressly excepting generic labels. A sketch may be a printer’s proof, hand drawing or computer-generated equivalent showing final features and placement.
1.establishes: The opening claim that government must have seen every label is incorrect. Special claims include undefined logos and trademarks, but the rule has defined exclusions. It governs approval before use; it does not demand a finished printer’s proof in every application.
1.relevance: This supports assessing the HMTc seal under the special-claim rules, not a guarantee of approval. The application needs Form 7234–1 and supporting records; the briefing’s five-item package is not an exhaustive checklist established here.

3.referenceTitle: 9 CFR 317.8 and 9 CFR 381.129 — False or misleading labeling or containers
3.citation: 9 CFR §§317.8 and 381.129, January 1, 2025 annual edition. Meat: false or misleading labeling and practices; poultry: false or misleading labeling or containers.
3.summary: Both provisions prohibit false or misleading labeling. Section 317.8(b)(34) specifically restricts “all,” “pure” and “100%” ingredient-content claims unless the product consists of a single ingredient.
3.establishes: The rules address context and accuracy rather than categorically banning the word “pure.” These two sections cover meat and poultry; they do not themselves supply the egg-product labeling provisions.
3.relevance: They support defining and substantiating a certification claim. They do not establish that HMTc will pass review, that every purity-related claim fails, or that named competitors had to redesign their seals.

4.referenceTitle: Food Standards and Labeling Policy Book
4.citation: USDA FSIS. Food Standards and Labeling Policy Book, revised September 8, 2025. Agency document reproduced by Penn State Agricultural Law.
4.summary: The policy book aims to help manufacturers create truthful labels. Its poultry and beef-patty entries describe circumstances allowing “all,” “pure” or “100 percent” claims. Its preface says compliance does not guarantee authorization.
4.establishes: The cited source supports specific composition qualifications, not a general ban on purity language. The reviewed entries do not document rejection of a heavy-metal certification seal or prove that a measured claim must be accepted.
4.relevance: The briefing should present its expected advantage as an inference. The source expressly limits any claim that preparing the described documentation ensures approval.

5.referenceTitle: Label Submission and Approval System (LSAS)
5.citation: USDA FSIS. Label Submission and Approval System (LSAS), public system information and contact page; FSIS overview last updated March 8, 2022.
5.summary: LSAS is FSIS’s electronic label-submission system. Its public portal identifies the Labeling and Program Delivery Staff and directs users to application support and the industry guide.
5.establishes: This establishes the system and its administrative purpose. A portal description does not prescribe HMTc’s exact certificate, licence, laboratory report and verification-address package, or guarantee a label decision.
5.relevance: LSAS is a supported route for submitting a label. The source does not show that the system requires the precise five documents proposed by this briefing or that a certifier receives blanket endorsement.

6.referenceTitle: Compliance Guideline for Label Approval
6.citation: USDA FSIS. FSIS Guideline for Label Approval, FSIS-GD-2025-0006, December 2025, replacing March 2024. Agency PDF reproduced by Penn State; issuance confirmed by USDA’s December 12, 2025 bulletin.
6.summary: The guidance distinguishes special claims from generic claims and allows blanket product-line approvals and some reuse after initial approval. It lists certified claims for review, but also includes some certification wording and qualified “pure” claims among generic examples.
6.establishes: This is nonbinding guidance. It does not document the briefing’s unnamed certifiers being forced to redraw purity seals. A claim’s actual content and the applicable approval route matter; certification wording alone does not settle every case.
6.relevance: It supports substantiation and label records, but qualifies the briefing’s assertion that each label always receives individual review. It supplies no approval, comparative success evidence or guaranteed filing recipe for HMTc.

7.referenceTitle: Heavy Metal Tested and Certified — Using the mark
7.citation: Heavy Metal Tested & Certified. Using the mark. Program-publisher webpage, accessed September 15, 2026.
7.summary: The page describes a product-specific mark based on a ten-analyte panel, native measurement basis, accredited laboratory testing, a three-lot baseline and ongoing surveillance. It requires scope information and rejects absolute-safety and zero-metal claims.
7.establishes: This is the program’s own representation of its rules. It is not independent verification that those rules are implemented, that a particular lot passes, or that FSIS has approved the mark or any label bearing it.
7.relevance: The source supports the intended meaning of the HMTc claim. The briefing’s prediction that this architecture will pass federal review remains an inference requiring an actual label and substantiation assessment.

1.referenceTitle: The Non-GMO Project and the Non-GMO Project Verified mark
1.citation: The Non-GMO Project. About the Non-GMO Project: mission and history. Organization website, accessed 15 September 2026.
1.summary: The organization describes its origins in two grocery stores, their joint founding of the Project in 2007, and the arrival of the first Butterfly-labeled products on shelves in 2010. It presents the mark as certification for GMO avoidance and describes its growth as rapid.
1.establishes: This first-party history supports the launch date and the program’s stated purpose. Its growth description is promotional self-reporting; it does not supply an audited comparison with USDA Organic, establish why shoppers chose the mark, or show that the Butterfly alone caused its growth.
1.relevance: The history supplies the concrete example behind this briefing’s analogy between a focused non-GMO mark and a focused heavy-metal mark. Applying that example to HMTc is a positioning argument, not evidence that HMTc will achieve similar recognition or that the heavy-metal category has no competing marks.

2.referenceTitle: National Organic Program
2.citation: United States. Organic Foods Production Act of 1990, Pub. L. 101-624, title XXI, enacted 28 November 1990, codified at 7 U.S.C. §§6501–6524 (2024 edition). U.S. Department of Agriculture, National Organic Program, 7 C.F.R. Part 205. USDA Agricultural Marketing Service, The Organic Integrity Quarterly, October 2012, pp. 1–2.
2.summary: The 1990 Act created a national framework for organic production and handling, certification and labeling. USDA’s implementing standards were fully implemented in October 2002. The rules govern farming and handling practices, allowed substances, inspections, residue testing and use of the organic label.
2.establishes: Organic certification verifies compliance with this production-and-handling system; it is not a general guarantee that finished foods are free of metals. The system nevertheless expressly addresses heavy-metal contamination prevention in soil-fertility management and provides for residue testing and contaminant reporting. Its scope should not be described as wholly silent on metals.
2.relevance: These sources establish the federal framework against which the briefing compares the later Non-GMO Project mark. They help distinguish an organic production claim from HMTc’s claim about measured concentrations, but do not establish universal shopper trust in 1990 or HMTc’s commercial ownership of a category.

3.referenceTitle: Total Diet Study, FY2018–2020
3.citation: U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Total Diet Study Report: Fiscal Years 2018–2020 Elements Data. July 2022.
3.summary: FDA measured nutrient and contaminant elements in retail foods, generally prepared for consumption. Its national monitoring results document detectable arsenic, cadmium, lead and mercury in parts of the food supply.
3.establishes: These are food-surveillance data, not a comparison of organic and conventional farming or verification of a particular brand. A nondetect means below the analytical reporting limit, not demonstrated absence. FDA does not take regulatory action from these composited TDS results.
3.relevance: The occurrence data explain why an organic or non-GMO label cannot by itself report a product’s measured metal concentrations. They support the briefing’s rationale for concentration evidence, while providing no comparison of certification-market positions, no measure of demand for HMTc, and no finding that farming practices never influence contamination.

4.referenceTitle: Hain Celestial Group, Inc. v. Palmquist
4.citation: Supreme Court of the United States. Hain Celestial Group, Inc. v. Palmquist, No. 24-724, 607 U.S. ___, decided 24 February 2026. California AB 899, Chapter 668, Statutes of 2023, adding Health and Safety Code §110962. Maryland Rudy’s Law, HB 97 / SB 723 (2024), codified at Health–General §21-330.4. U.S. House Committee on Oversight and Reform, Subcommittee on Economic and Consumer Policy. Baby Foods Are Tainted with Dangerous Levels of Arsenic, Lead, Cadmium, and Mercury. California phased in testing in 2024 and disclosure in 2025; Maryland phased them in during 2025 and 2026, within each law’s defined scope. The House report makes findings and recommendations. None measures demand for a heavy-metal seal or requires HMTc certification.
4.relevance: The materials explain the legal and public-information setting for the briefing’s proposed heavy-metal market position. 6.citation: Pendergrass, Karen. The Cost of Operating Without Credible Third-Party Heavy-Metal Certification. Journal of Food Metallomics, preprint, 7 March 2026, pp. 1–6. doi: 10.5281/zenodo.18903738.
6.summary: This paper combines contamination, recall, litigation and retailer evidence in illustrative business-loss scenarios. Section 7.3 estimates first-year costs of $1.6M–$6.6M or more for a $5M-revenue brand experiencing a public heavy-metals event, including recall, legal, sales, distribution and remediation costs.
6.establishes: These are modeled scenarios by the briefing’s author, not observed losses for a representative group of premium brands. The model assumes incident severity, sales disruption and certification benefits; it does not independently measure how much HMTc reduces event risk or establish a guaranteed return.
6.relevance: It provides the scenario behind this briefing’s financial-exposure example and a framework for weighing verification costs against potential disruption. A brand would need its own incident probability, margins, channel exposure and program costs to assess the business case.

7.referenceTitle: HMTc Infant and Child Foods Program Manual
7.citation: Pendergrass, Karen. Heavy Metal Tested & Certified (HMTc) Infant and Child Foods Program Manual. 2026 edition, v0. The Paleo Foundation, 18 May 2026. doi:10.5281/zenodo.20270512. This is the cited first deposit; later editions supersede it.
7.summary: The manual specifies HMTc’s infant-food certification framework: product testing, surveillance, corrective action and restrictions on use of the certification mark. The cited edition also compares the program with USDA Organic, Non-GMO Project and other certification or testing programs.
7.establishes: Parts 2.1 and 2.5 treat action levels as tools for managing contamination and prohibit claims of absolute safety, zero metals or zero risk. These are HMTc program requirements, not government law or independent evidence that certification prevents injury, litigation or loss of consumer trust.
7.relevance: It supplies the program rules behind this briefing’s argument for making verifiable claims: describe testing against stated limits and continuing surveillance, while avoiding a promise of safety. Its comparison of certification scopes explains why an organic or non-GMO badge cannot stand in for verification of metal concentrations.

1.referenceTitle: Baby Foods Are Tainted with Dangerous Levels of Arsenic, Lead, Cadmium, and Mercury
1.citation: U.S. House Committee on Oversight and Reform, Subcommittee on Economic and Consumer Policy. Staff report, 4 February 2021.
1.summary: Congressional staff examined company testing records for arsenic, lead, cadmium and mercury in baby foods and recommended finished-product testing and public disclosure.
1.establishes: It documents the investigation's four-metal scope. It does not establish a complete testing panel, industry-wide certification practice or subsequent litigation history.
1.relevance: It grounds the briefing's opening discussion of the familiar four metals. The later claim about multidistrict litigation needs a separate court source; the case for testing additional elements rests on the other cited assessments and standards.

2.referenceTitle: Closer to Zero: Reducing Childhood Exposure to Contaminants from Foods
2.citation: U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Closer to Zero: Reducing Childhood Exposure to Contaminants from Foods. Initiative launched 2021; living program page.
2.summary: FDA’s Closer to Zero initiative addresses children’s dietary exposure to lead, arsenic, cadmium and mercury. Its process combines research, assessment, consultation and development of action levels.
2.establishes: This establishes the initiative’s four-contaminant focus. It does not define all contaminants regulated by FDA or establish the scope of every commercial certification.
2.relevance: The initiative explains the four-metal reference point used in this briefing. HMTc’s wider panel is a separate program choice, not a requirement imposed by Closer to Zero.

3.referenceTitle: Commission Recommendation (EU) 2024/907 of 22 March 2024 on the monitoring of nickel in food
3.citation: European Commission. Commission Recommendation (EU) 2024/907 of 22 March 2024 on the monitoring of nickel in food. OJ L, 26 March 2024.
3.summary: The Commission recommends that Member States, working with food businesses, monitor nickel during 2025–2027 in named foods including cocoa, chocolate, cereals, soy products, pulses and nuts. It also recommends mitigation work and reporting occurrence data to EFSA.
3.establishes: The recommendation responds to both chronic dietary exposure and acute reactions in nickel-sensitized people. It is a monitoring recommendation, distinct from a regulation setting binding commodity limits.
3.relevance: It supports HMTc’s attention to nickel and identifies relevant food matrices. It does not require HMTc certification or a universal eight-metal panel.

4.referenceTitle: Update of the risk assessment of nickel in food and drinking water
4.citation: EFSA Panel on Contaminants in the Food Chain (CONTAM). Update of the risk assessment of nickel in food and drinking water. EFSA Journal. 2020;18(11):6268. doi:10.2903/j.efsa.2020.6268.
4.summary: Using more than 47,000 occurrence results, EFSA set a chronic nickel tolerable daily intake of 13 µg/kg body weight, based on post-implantation loss in rats. It separately assessed acute oral exposure causing systemic contact dermatitis in nickel-sensitized people.
4.establishes: High-percentile dietary estimates exceeded the chronic benchmark in many child surveys; average exposure was generally below it. These are population exposure benchmarks and modeled risks, not food concentration limits or proof of individual injury.
4.relevance: The assessment supports including nickel in HMTc’s hazard review while requiring separate treatment of chronic intake, sensitized consumers and commodity limits.

5.referenceTitle: Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code, Schedule 19 — Maximum levels of contaminants and natural toxicants
5.citation: Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code, Schedule 19—Maximum levels of contaminants and natural toxicants, instrument F2015L00454; compilation 13 September 2024, §§S19–3 and S19–4. FSANZ, Proposal P1028 implementation information.
5.summary: Schedule 19 sets commodity-specific metal limits. The reviewed 2024 compilation lists aluminium at 0.5 mg/kg for specified infant formula products,1 mg/kg for soy-based formula and 0.2 mg/kg for preterm special-medical products; canned-food tin is 250 mg/kg.
5.establishes: These are food concentration limits with defined product and preparation rules. The 2024 infant-formula revision applies in Australia, with a transition to 13 September 2029; New Zealand opted out of that revision.
5.relevance: The Code provides a concrete example of aluminium regulation beyond the familiar four metals. HMTc comparisons must identify jurisdiction, edition, formula class and concentration basis.

6.referenceTitle: National Food Safety Standard — Maximum Levels of Contaminants in Foods, GB 2762-2022
6.citation: National Health Commission and State Administration for Market Regulation of China. GB 2762-2022, National Food Safety Standard—Maximum Levels of Contaminants in Foods. Issued 30 June 2022; effective 30 June 2023. Reviewed through USDA FAS unofficial translation CH2023-0040; supersession checked against GB 2762-2025 translation CH2025-0202.
6.summary: The 2022 standard sets limits for named contaminants and food categories, including tin, nickel and total chromium. Tin limits apply to tinplate-packed foods; nickel limits concern hydrogenated vegetable oils and related products; chromium limits cover specified commodity groups.
6.establishes: It supports the presence of these additional metals in Chinese food regulation, not a requirement to test every food for all of them. The 2022 edition has been replaced by GB 2762-2025, effective 2 September 2026.
6.relevance: HMTc can use these rules as jurisdiction-specific context for a broader panel. It must distinguish total chromium from Cr(VI), and current law from the 2022 edition cited in this briefing.

7.referenceTitle: Regulation in India of Heavy Metals in Food Items: A Critical Analysis
7.citation: Sadhya M, Saha M. Regulation in India of Heavy Metals in Food Items: A Critical Analysis. Environmental Analysis & Ecology Studies. 2023;11(5):000771. Published 21 December 2023. doi:10.31031/EAES.2023.11.000771.
7.summary: This legal review discusses India’s food-safety framework and reproduces selected contaminant limits from the 2011 regulations. Its table includes tin for specified canned foods, chromium for fishery products and nickel for specified processed vegetable oils and fats.
7.establishes: The article establishes what its authors reported about those rules in 2023. It is not enacted law, a current consolidated regulatory schedule or an original exposure study.
7.relevance: It provides context for HMTc’s comparison with Indian contaminant regulation. Any operational limits require checking the governing current instrument and exact food category.

8.referenceTitle: Hexavalent Chromium Maximum Contaminant Level (10 µg/L)
8.citation: California State Water Resources Control Board. Hexavalent Chromium MCL, rulemaking SWRCB-DDW-21-003, effective 1 October 2024. California OEHHA. Public Health Goal for Hexavalent Chromium in Drinking Water. July 2011.
8.summary: California’s rule establishes a drinking-water maximum contaminant level of 10 µg/L for Cr(VI), with system-size compliance dates in 2026–2028. OEHHA’s separate 2011 public-health goal is 0.02 µg/L, based on cancer-risk assessment.
8.establishes: The enforceable MCL and health goal have different legal roles. They concern drinking water, not chromium limits for packaged food; the health goal is not itself an enforceable standard.
8.relevance: These sources illustrate why HMTc should distinguish chemical species and exposure routes. Neither value can be transferred directly to food or treated as a certification mandate.
