9.referenceTitle: Proposition 65 list (Safe Drinking Water and Toxic Enforcement Act of 1986)
9.citation: California Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment. The Proposition 65 List. Nickel and chromium entries, accessed 15 September 2026.
9.summary: OEHHA lists metallic nickel and nickel compounds for cancer, soluble nickel compounds for developmental and male reproductive toxicity, and hexavalent chromium compounds for cancer and reproductive/developmental toxicity.
9.establishes: The entries identify listed chemical forms, endpoints and listing dates. Listing alone does not supply a universal food concentration cap, prove an exposure is unlawful or show a particular food caused cancer.
9.relevance: For HMTc’s panel discussion, the list is a reason to assess nickel and chromium species and applicable exposure duties. It does not replace food-specific risk assessment.

10.referenceTitle: Nickel Content of Food and Estimation of Dietary Intake
10.citation: Flyvholm MA, Nielsen GD, Andersen A. Nickel content of food and estimation of dietary intake. Zeitschrift für Lebensmittel-Untersuchung und-Forschung. 1984;179(6):427–431. doi:10.1007/BF01043419.
10.summary: This review identifies cocoa/chocolate, soybeans, oatmeal, nuts and legumes as foods with high nickel content, and discusses estimated Danish dietary intake and possible eczema flare-ups after oral exposure.
10.establishes: The accessible abstract supports these foods as nickel sources. It does not establish a current global ranking with cocoa above every common food or oats near the top in all markets.
10.relevance: It provides historical context for HMTc to consider nickel in relevant ingredient matrices. Current testing and newer occurrence assessments are needed for product-specific decisions.

11.referenceTitle: Association between nickel exposure and diabetes risk: an updated meta-analysis of observational studies
11.citation: Lu H, Shi X, Han L, Liu X, Jiang Q. Association between nickel exposure and diabetes risk: an updated meta-analysis of observational studies. Frontiers in Public Health. 2024;12:1463880. Published 5 November 2024. doi:10.3389/fpubh.2024.1463880.
11.summary: The meta-analysis pooled 19 observational studies involving 46,071 participants. Urinary nickel showed a weak positive association with diabetes; blood nickel did not show a significant overall association.
11.establishes: This is biomarker-based observational evidence, largely cross-sectional. It does not establish that dietary nickel causes diabetes, quantify a food limit or show that certification prevents disease.
11.relevance: It extends the research context for HMTc’s nickel review, while the briefing’s commercial argument must remain separate from the association and its uncertainties.

12.referenceTitle: Safety of aluminium from dietary intake — Scientific Opinion
12.citation: EFSA Panel on Food Additives, Flavourings, Processing Aids and Food Contact Materials (AFC). Safety of aluminium from dietary intake. EFSA Journal. 2008;754:1–34. Adopted 22 May 2008; published 15 July 2008. doi:10.2903/j.efsa.2008.754.
12.summary: EFSA established a tolerable weekly aluminium intake of 1 mg/kg body weight from all dietary sources, drawing on animal neurodevelopmental and reproductive studies and aluminium’s persistence in the body. Estimated intake could exceed this benchmark for part of the European population.
12.establishes: The benchmark is an aggregate weekly exposure value, not a universal aluminium concentration limit for formula. The assessment also states that available data did not show dietary aluminium to constitute an Alzheimer’s-disease risk.
12.relevance: It supports considering aluminium in HMTc’s exposure review while preserving the difference between hazard assessment, an intake benchmark and a product pass/fail rule.

13.referenceTitle: The Health Effects of Aluminum Exposure
13.citation: Klotz K, Weistenhöfer W, Neff F, Hartwig A, van Thriel C, Drexler H. The Health Effects of Aluminum Exposure. Deutsches Ärzteblatt International. 2017;114(39):653–659. doi:10.3238/arztebl.2017.0653.
13.summary: This selective review evaluates aluminium exposure from environmental, occupational and therapeutic settings. It distinguishes demonstrated high-exposure neurotoxicity from unresolved claims about Alzheimer’s disease and breast cancer.
13.establishes: Occupational biomarkers and dialysis exposure are not equivalent to ordinary dietary intake. The review does not establish that aluminium in any particular formula causes neurological disease.
13.relevance: It gives HMTc’s aluminium discussion needed dose-and-route context. Monitoring rationale should not turn high-exposure evidence into an unqualified claim about all detectable food aluminium.

14.referenceTitle: Commission Regulation (EU) No 380/2012 of 3 May 2012 amending Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008 as regards the conditions of use and the use levels for aluminium-containing food additives
14.citation: European Commission. Commission Regulation (EU)  No. 380/2012 of 3 May 2012 amending Annex II to Regulation (EC)  No 1333/2008 as regards conditions of use and use levels for aluminium-containing food additives. OJ L119, 4 May 2012.
14.summary: This regulation narrowed permissions and levels for specified aluminium-containing food additives, including aluminium lakes, in response to EFSA’s dietary-intake assessment.
14.establishes: It is a binding amendment to additive authorizations with specific application and transition dates. It is not a general contaminant ceiling for all aluminium in every food.
14.relevance: It illustrates a regulatory response beyond the four-metal panel. HMTc should distinguish intentionally used additives and their authorized conditions from measured total aluminium contamination.

15.referenceTitle: Prescription Infant Formulas Are Contaminated with Aluminium
15.citation: Redgrove J, Rodriguez I, Mahadevan-Bava S, Exley C. Prescription Infant Formulas Are Contaminated with Aluminium. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. 2019;16(5):899. doi:10.3390/ijerph16050899.
15.summary: The authors measured total aluminium in 24 prescription formula/nutrition products obtained from a UK pediatric clinic. Ready-to-drink concentrations ranged approximately 50–1,956 µg/L, and powdered products also varied.
15.establishes: The roughly 39-fold ready-to-drink range supports variation among sampled products. This small product survey did not measure infant health outcomes or establish current market-wide levels; powders and liquids have different reporting bases.
15.relevance: It supports HMTc’s interest in measuring aluminium in specialist nutrition products. It does not demonstrate a certification benefit, a universal infant dose threshold or that every sampled product served the same clinical purpose.

16.referenceTitle: Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 of 25 April 2023 on maximum levels for certain contaminants in food and repealing Regulation (EC) No 1881/2006
16.citation: European Commission. Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 of 25 April 2023 on maximum levels for certain contaminants in food and repealing Regulation (EC) No 1881/2006. OJ L119, 5 May 2023, pp 103–157; Annex I §3.5.
16.summary: The original regulation sets inorganic-tin maxima of 200 mg/kg for covered canned foods and 100 mg/kg for covered canned beverages, with 50 mg/kg for specified canned infant/young-child and medical foods.
16.establishes: These are category-specific binding limits. Infant provisions exclude canned dried/powdered products; general food and beverage limits use wet weight. They do not regulate all tin species or all food packaging identically.
16.relevance: The rule supplies an actual tin benchmark for HMTc’s comparison. Its narrower infant categories and speciation prevent treating the page’s shorthand as a universal global standard.

17.referenceTitle: General Standard for Contaminants and Toxins in Food and Feed
17.citation: Codex Alimentarius Commission. General Standard for Contaminants and Toxins in Food and Feed, CXS193-1995. Adopted 1995; reviewed consolidated version last amended 2025, tin table, p75.
17.summary: Codex recommends maximum tin levels of 250 mg/kg for canned foods other than beverages and 150 mg/kg for canned beverages, with additional provisions for specified meat products in non-tinplate containers.
17.establishes: The standard’s scope expressly describes recommendations for international trade, not automatically binding national law. Its tin definition defaults to total tin unless otherwise specified; its table does not establish a general 50 mg/kg infant-food limit.
17.relevance: Codex helps HMTc compare food-category rules and the reasons for tin surveillance. It does not establish complete global harmonization or mandate an eight-metal certificate.

18.referenceTitle: Occurrence of Tin in Foods and Dietary Exposure Assessment in Zhejiang Province, China
18.citation: Ye S, Chen J, Zhang R, et al. Occurrence of Tin in Foods and Dietary Exposure Assessment in Zhejiang Province, China. Foods. 2026;15(6):982. Published 10 March 2026. doi:10.3390/foods15060982.
18.summary: The study measured total tin in 2,014 samples from five food categories in Zhejiang and combined concentrations with dietary-survey data. Canned foods had higher concentrations than most fresh foods, while modeled total-tin hazard quotients remained below 1.
18.establishes: It is regional occurrence and modeled-exposure evidence. Organotin risks were explored through assumed fractions and scenarios, not measured organotin speciation; it does not demonstrate universal high risk or causal leaching in each sample.
18.relevance: It supports HMTc’s focus on packaging and product matrix when deciding tin surveillance. Its generally low total-tin estimates and modeling limitations belong alongside the briefing’s concern about canned foods.

19.referenceTitle: Genetic and Epigenetic Mechanisms in Metal Carcinogenesis and Cocarcinogenesis: Nickel, Arsenic, and Chromium
19.citation: Salnikow K, Zhitkovich A. Genetic and Epigenetic Mechanisms in Metal Carcinogenesis and Cocarcinogenesis: Nickel, Arsenic, and Chromium. Chemical Research in Toxicology. 2008;21(1):28–44. Online 30 October 2007. doi:10.1021/tx700198a.
19.summary: This mechanistic review describes different carcinogenic processes for nickel, inorganic arsenic and Cr(VI). For chromium, cellular uptake and reduction explain why oxidation state and where reduction occurs matter.
19.establishes: The reviewed chromium section describes sulfate-channel entry, extracellular reduction to poorly permeable Cr(III), and intracellular reduction that can generate genotoxic damage. Mechanistic evidence does not quantify risk from a particular food concentration.
19.relevance: It supports HMTc’s attention to chromium speciation. A total-chromium result alone cannot identify oxidation state, but the review does not demonstrate the prevalence of Cr(VI) in food or validate an HMTc method.

20.referenceTitle: Adverse Human Health Effects of Chromium by Exposure Route: A Comprehensive Review Based on Toxicogenomic Approach
20.citation: Shin DY, Lee SM, Jang Y, Lee J, Lee CM, Cho EM, Seo YR. Adverse Human Health Effects of Chromium by Exposure Route: A Comprehensive Review Based on Toxicogenomic Approach. International Journal of Molecular Sciences. 2023;24(4):3410. doi:10.3390/ijms24043410.
20.summary: The authors review dermal, inhalation and ingestion evidence and analyze public gene-expression datasets to propose route-related chromium toxicity pathways. The ingestion analysis uses Cr(VI)-exposed mouse duodenum data.
20.establishes: The findings support route-specific assessment and mechanistic hypotheses. They do not establish that workplace lung-cancer evidence transfers directly to food ingestion or that predicted gene networks prove human disease.
20.relevance: For HMTc, this helps explain why a chromium source drawer must distinguish skin, air, drinking water and food. It does not establish a finished-food limit or certify analytical performance.

21.referenceTitle: Scientific Opinion on the risks to public health related to the presence of chromium in food and drinking water
21.citation: EFSA CONTAM Panel. Scientific Opinion on the risks to public health related to the presence of chromium in food and drinking water. EFSA Journal. 2014;12(3):3595. Adopted 27 February 2014; corrected 12 June 2014 version replacing 13 March 2014 publication. doi:10.2903/j.efsa.2014.3595.
21.summary: EFSA treated reported food chromium as Cr(III) because oxidation-state occurrence data were unavailable and food is generally reducing. It evaluated drinking-water Cr(VI) separately and called for better species-specific data.
21.establishes: The 2014 opinion reported no standardized Cr(VI) food method or proficiency scheme, while identifying chromatography with ICP-MS and species-specific isotope dilution as useful speciation tools. This is not evidence that Cr(VI) in food cannot be measured today.
21.relevance: It supports HMTc’s requirement to justify speciation methods and matrices. It also limits the briefing’s present-tense claims about analytical impossibility and the absence of worldwide food rules.

22.referenceTitle: In re: Baby Food Products Liability Litigation
22.citation: In re Baby Food Products Liability Litigation, No. 3:24-md-03101-JSC (N.D. Cal.), Doc 447, Amended Order re Defendants’ Motions to Dismiss and Motion to Strike, filed 2 April 2025, pp 29–32.
22.summary: The court struck aluminium references from the master complaint after plaintiffs said they did not intend to pursue those claims and the court confirmed they would not be addressed in the MDL. The order separately discusses infant-formula scope.
22.establishes: This is a pleading and litigation-scope ruling, not a finding that aluminium is safe or cannot cause injury. The infant-formula ruling in this document is expressly tentative and permits separate litigation or a request to the JPML.
22.relevance: It demonstrates that HMTc’s chosen analyte scope need not match this MDL’s pleaded claims. It does not establish a toxicological standard or guarantee that certification changes legal outcomes.

23.referenceTitle: Proposition 65 industry-wide settlement on hexavalent chromium in chrome-tanned leather footwear and gloves
23.citation: Center for Environmental Health v. Bali Leathers, Inc., et al., lead case RG19-029736(Alameda County Superior Court). Consent judgment reported 21 February 2024; California Attorney General notice record 2020-03394. CEH settlement account, 7 March 2024.
23.summary: An industry settlement addressed Cr(VI) exposure from chrome-tanned footwear and gloves. CEH describes sourcing requirements intended to prevent surface Cr(VI), including specified tannery protocols or qualifying Leather Working Group audits.
23.establishes: The reviewed Attorney General record confirms a settlement-based judgment and warning/reformulation relief. This is a leather skin-contact matter, not a food regulation or a ruling validating HMTc.
23.relevance: It illustrates a practical enforcement setting for chromium species, while the briefing’s food-panel argument remains an analogy across distinct products and exposure routes.

24.referenceTitle: People of the State of California v. McWane, Inc. (dba AB&I Foundry)
24.citation: People of the State of California v. McWane, Inc., dba AB&I, No. 22CV007067 (Alameda County Superior Court). Complaint for Injunctive Relief and Civil Penalties, filed 15 February 2022.
24.summary: The Attorney General alleged that an East Oakland foundry emitted Cr(VI) into surrounding air without required warnings and sought relief under Proposition 65 and other state law.
24.establishes: The complaint establishes allegations and requested remedies, not proven liability or food contamination. Its inhalation exposure and industrial-emission setting differ from dietary exposure.
24.relevance: It provides a concrete chromium enforcement example relevant to HMTc’s broader hazard discussion. It cannot establish that a chromium result in food violates the same provisions or that certification prevents a lawsuit.

25.referenceTitle: HMTc Infant and Child Foods Program Manual
25.citation: Pendergrass K. HMTc Infant and Child Foods Program Manual. 2026 edition. Edition comparison: deposited v0, 18 May 2026, doi:10.5281/zenodo.20270512; Institute of Contaminant Standards, current 2026 web edition dated 6 August 2026, consolidated v2 PDF.
25.summary: The manual defines HMTc’s private certification scope and testing rules. The earlier deposited edition describes eight elements and ten analytes; the current web volume uses total chromium with conditional Cr(VI) speciation and distinguishes its limit panel from reflex tests.
25.establishes: This establishes stated program requirements, not independently demonstrated health protection or a government mandate. The citation does not pin an edition, and the program’s own current description differs from the briefing’s fixed ten-analyte wording.
25.relevance: It is the primary source for HMTc’s proposed broader coverage. A defensible comparison must name the edition and distinguish core measurements from matrix- or pathway-triggered speciation.

1.referenceTitle: In re: Baby Food Products Liability Litigation
1.citation: U.S. Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation. In re: Baby Food Products Liability Litigation, MDL No. 3101, Transfer Order, 11 April 2024. Transferred to the Northern District of California, No. 3:24-md-03101-JSC.
1.summary: The Judicial Panel centralized related baby-food personal-injury actions in the Northern District of California for coordinated or consolidated pretrial proceedings before Judge Jacqueline Scott Corley.
1.establishes: The transfer order establishes the litigation’s organization and common alleged factual issues. Centralization does not establish causation, product defect or liability, and this order contains no ruling excluding experts.
1.relevance: It identifies the federal proceeding invoked in the briefing’s opening. HMTc’s proposed surveillance record is separate from the procedural decision to coordinate these cases, and its value as evidence still depends on the governing legal requirements.

2.referenceTitle: In re: Baby Food Products Liability Litigation
2.citation: U.S. District Court, Northern District of California. In re: Baby Food Products Liability Litigation, No. 3:24-md-03101-JSC, Document 710, Order re Defendants’ Motion to Exclude Plaintiffs’ Expert Witnesses, 27 February 2026 (Jacqueline Scott Corley, J.). This verified order differs from the December 2025 date stated in the bibliography.
2.summary: After hearings in December 2025, the court excluded specified menu opinions, exposure calculations and epidemiology/toxicology causation opinions under Rule 702. It permitted Dr. Kevin Shapiro’s more limited opinions, which did not offer a general-causation conclusion.
2.establishes: The order evaluates the reliability and fit of the offered opinions in the ASD/ADHD litigation. It neither holds all heavy-metal exposure harmless nor allows testing histories to replace required causation evidence. It resolves the identified expert motions, not a final judgment on every claim.
2.relevance: It illustrates why scientifically supported exposure assumptions and an intelligible testing record can matter. The briefing’s claim that the case therefore shifts to a jury question answerable without a toxicologist is an HMTc litigation interpretation, not this order’s holding.

3.referenceTitle: Hain Celestial Group, Inc. v. Palmquist
3.citation: Supreme Court of the United States. Hain Celestial Group, Inc. v. Palmquist, No. 24-724, 607 U.S. ___, decided 24 February 2026 (Sotomayor, J., for a unanimous Court).
3.summary: The Supreme Court considered whether a federal judgment could survive when a nondiverse retailer had been improperly dismissed from a removed baby-food case. It held that the dismissal did not cure the original jurisdictional defect.
3.establishes: The Court affirmed the appellate judgment requiring the federal judgment to be vacated and the case returned to state court. It decided jurisdiction, not injury causation or liability, and did not mandate certification or a particular testing protocol.
3.relevance: The case supplies the forum context for the briefing’s advice about preserving testing records. HMTc’s suggested defensive advantage is separate from the jurisdictional holding; the opinion does not show that documented compliance wins a case or removes the need for expert evidence.

4.referenceTitle: Palmer v. Hoffman
4.citation: Supreme Court of the United States. Palmer v. Hoffman, 318 U.S. 109, 111–115 (1943), decided 1 February 1943 (Douglas, J.).
4.summary: The Court upheld exclusion of a railroad engineer’s post-accident statement under the predecessor federal business-records statute. Regularly collecting such statements did not make this report a record of ordinary railroad operations.
4.establishes: The Court focused on the report’s operational purpose and reliability, rather than routine creation alone. The decision predates the Federal Rules of Evidence and is not a rule that every post-dispute record is inadmissible or every pre-dispute record admissible.
4.relevance: It supports examining why HMTc testing records were created and how they were used in routine quality operations. Timing can be relevant, but the briefing’s claim that before-versus-after litigation alone determines opposite admissibility outcomes is broader than the holding.

5.referenceTitle: Fed. R. Evid. 803(6)
5.citation: Federal Rules of Evidence, Rule 803(6)(A)–(E), Records of a Regularly Conducted Activity; see also Rule 902(11)–(12). Official rules compilation, 1 December 2025.
5.summary: Rule 803(6) provides a hearsay exception for qualifying records made near the event by a knowledgeable person, kept in a regularly conducted activity and routinely made. A qualified witness or prescribed certification must establish the required foundation.
5.establishes: The opponent may show that the information source or preparation circumstances lack trustworthiness. A pre-existing testing schedule does not satisfy every condition by itself. The legal certification contemplated by Rule 902 is a records-foundation procedure, not an HMTc product seal.
5.relevance: HMTc’s continuing records could help document routine preparation and informed recordkeeping. Counsel would still need the actual evidence, an adequate foundation and consideration of other objections; certification does not make a surveillance file automatically admissible or self-authenticating.

6.referenceTitle: Cal. Evid. Code § 1271
6.citation: California Evidence Code §1271, Business Records (enacted by Stats. 1965, ch. 299), official codified text accessed 15 September 2026.
6.summary: Section 1271 provides a hearsay exception for a qualifying business record made near the event in the regular course of business. A custodian or other qualified witness must identify the writing and explain its preparation, and its sources and preparation must indicate trustworthiness.
6.establishes: All four statutory conditions matter. Routine surveillance can help establish some conditions, but neither an HMTc seal nor creation before litigation establishes the entire foundation. A California venue alone does not make this state rule govern a federal MDL.
6.relevance: The provision is relevant when HMTc testing records are offered in a proceeding governed by California evidence law. It supports documenting the record’s origin and preparation without promising admission or assuming identical rules across state and federal cases.

7.referenceTitle: Fed. R. Evid. 901
7.citation: Federal Rules of Evidence, Rule 901(a), (b)(1), (b)(9); see Rule 902(11). Official compilation, 1 December 2025. ISO/IEC 17025:2017, General requirements for the competence of testing and calibration laboratories, third edition, November 2017.
7.summary: Rule 901 requires evidence sufficient to support that an item is what its proponent claims. Examples include a knowledgeable witness and evidence explaining an accurate process or system. ISO/IEC 17025 separately provides a laboratory-competence and impartiality benchmark.
7.establishes: Laboratory accreditation and custody documentation may contribute to a foundation, but Rule 901 does not mandate that particular combination or guarantee admission. Authentication also does not establish the truth of every result, resolve hearsay objections or prevent cross-examination.
7.relevance: The sources explain why HMTc should preserve sample identity, handling records and laboratory methods. Whether a particular report is authenticated remains a legal and factual question; the program’s rule invalidating a result after a custody break is not an automatic court exclusion rule.

1.referenceTitle: T-4-93 — Safety Standards for Fertilizers and Supplements
1.citation: Canadian Food Inspection Agency. T-4-93: Safety standards for fertilizers and supplements. Modified 22 November 2024; section 3.1 and Table 1.
1.summary: CFIA derives product metal concentrations from maximum annual application rates and acceptable additions to soil over 45 years. The standards cover total metal content in fertilizers and supplements, including processed sewage and compost.
1.establishes: The cumulative cadmium allowance is 4 kg/ha; the example 20 mg/kg product concentration assumes 4,400 kg/ha annually. Application rate and concentration must use the same dry or as-is basis. This is not a universal food limit.
1.relevance: It supports considering input history alongside HMTc product testing. The Canadian calculation does not establish that every jurisdiction uses a 45-year horizon or that a finished-product test cannot detect soil-derived contamination.

2.referenceTitle: Regulation (EU) 2019/1009 laying down rules on the making available on the market of EU fertilising products
2.citation: European Parliament and Council. Regulation (EU) 2019/1009 of 5 June 2019 laying down rules on the making available on the market of EU fertilising products. OJ L 170, 25 June 2019, pp. 1–114; original act.
2.summary: The original act sets category-specific contaminant limits for EU fertilising products. Inorganic phosphate fertilizers with at least 5% phosphorus-pentoxide equivalent have a 60 mg/kg P₂O₅ cadmium limit; qualifying low-cadmium labeling uses 20 mg/kg P₂O₅.
2.establishes: The act generally applies from 16 July 2022 and called for a review by July 2026, without automatically lowering the limit. These are composition rules with specified categories and bases, not a shared 45-year cumulative-loading formula.
2.relevance: It supports examining fertilizer composition as an upstream input. It does not prove the source of a particular food result or validate HMTc’s testing frequency; current compliance also requires applicable amendments and national provisions.

3.referenceTitle: 40 CFR Part 503 — Standards for the Use or Disposal of Sewage Sludge

3.relevance: They support tracing biosolids inputs and application records. HMTc must keep these environmental controls separate from food specifications and cannot infer a particular field’s history or a food’s compliance from this rule alone.

5.referenceTitle: Wastewater-Irrigation Multi-Metal Crop Pathway (evidence synthesis)
5.citation: Pendergrass, Karen. Wastewater and sewage-effluent irrigation is a single upstream pathway that co-elevates multiple metals in the same crop, concentrating in leafy greens on peri-urban plots across the Global South. 5.summary: The synthesis connects five sources on irrigation-related crop contamination, including a lead meta-analysis, field surveys and a controlled arsenic-irrigation experiment.
5.establishes: It is an author’s interpretation, with no external review recorded on the examined page. The arsenic experiment models geogenic groundwater rather than sewage, and the evidence does not uniformly isolate irrigation from other inputs.

6.referenceTitle: Meta-Analysis of Public Health Risks of Lead Accumulation in the Wastewater, Irrigated Soil, and Crops Nexus
6.citation: Ali, Adane Sirage; Bayih, Argaw Ambelu; and Gari, Sirak Robele. Meta-analysis of public health risks of lead accumulation in wastewater, irrigated soil, and crops nexus. Frontiers in Public Health 10:977721, 18 October 2022. doi:10.3389/fpubh.2022.977721.

6.establishes: Between-study heterogeneity was very high (I²=98%). The review concerns lead, not a pooled multi-metal effect; its modeled risk indices are not observations of illness or proof of a particular causal source.
6.relevance: It supports attention to wastewater-linked sourcing risks. It does not demonstrate that every affected crop exceeds current law or that a four-metal finished-product test would miss the lead it measures.

7.citation: Adebayo RK, Hassan UF, Adamu HM, Hassan HF, Baba H, Ajiya DA. Levels of heavy metals and their health risk assessment from wastewater irrigated spinach in railway quarters, Bauchi, Bauchi state, Nigeria. 7.summary: The authors analyzed irrigation water and dried edible African spinach from one Bauchi farm. Reported spinach concentrations included lead 6.60, cadmium 1.00 and nickel 7.70 mg/kg.

1.referenceTitle: Lead Astray? The Hidden Contaminants in the Australian Anabolic–Androgenic Steroid Market and Their Potential Health Impact
1.citation: Craven A, Ferris J, Nielsen S, Piatkowski T. Lead Astray? The Hidden Contaminants in Australian Anabolic–Androgenic Steroid Market and Their Potential Health Impact. Drug and Alcohol Review. 2025. doi:10.1111/dar.70007. Version of record, seven-page brief report.
1.summary: Researchers tested 28 anonymously donated anabolic-steroid products reportedly purchased in Australia during 2022–2024: 16 injectable oils, 10 oral products and two powders. Fifteen were mislabeled or missold; four of 21 with stated expected doses were within ±5%. ICP-OES testing found metals in all three product classes.
1.establishes: This small convenience sample establishes composition problems in the tested AAS products, not market-wide rates for peptides or SARMs. Metal concentration must be combined with product dose to estimate daily exposure; the study did not measure patient injury or manufacturing practices.
1.relevance: It supports investigating an additional source of risk in AAS. Extending its findings to other synthetic products, or claiming that HMTc certification reduces clinical harm, requires additional evidence.

2.referenceTitle: ICH Q3D(R2) Guideline for Elemental Impurities
2.citation: International Council for Harmonisation. Guideline for Elemental Impurities Q3D(R2). Step 4, 2022; document history includes April 2022 corrections. Sections 2–6 and Appendix 2, Table A.2.1.
2.summary: Q3D supplies route-specific permitted daily exposures and a risk-based strategy for controlling elemental impurities in finished drug products. Its scope includes specified protein and synthetic-polypeptide drug products, with listed exclusions. Testing is one possible control rather than a universal requirement for every component or batch.
2.establishes: Daily exposure values are not standalone concentration limits. Oral/parenteral PDEs include cadmium 5/2, mercury 30/3 and nickel 200/20 µg/day; lead is 5/5 and arsenic 15/15. A lower parenteral value is therefore not universal. The guideline does not provide an aluminum PDE.
2.relevance: It supplies toxicological reference points for HMTc’s proposed dose-based assessment. Every-lot testing and a particular rule for nasal, sublingual or troche products are HMTc decisions, not blanket Q3D requirements.

1.referenceTitle: Lead concentrations in commercial dogfood containing pheasant in the UK
1.citation: Pain DJ, Green RE, Bates N, Guiu M, Taggart MA. Ambio. 2023;52:1339–1349. Published 3 May 2023. doi:10.1007/s13280-023-01856-x.
1.summary: The UK study tested 185 packages across eight game-meat and chicken dog-food products using X-rays and ICP-OES. Raw pheasant products had highly variable lead; the weighted mean after excluding known whole-shot samples was about 221 mg/kg dry weight.
1.establishes: The 34-fold comparison is with pheasant sold for human consumption, not background contamination. The three raw-product exceedance rates of 63–100% concern applicable feed maxima. This retail study did not test health outcomes or all raw diets.
1.relevance: It supports ingredient-specific testing of game-based pet food. Human-food comparisons need the correct matrix, moisture basis and legal scope; neither a comparison nor certification demonstrates veterinary benefit.

2.referenceTitle: Individual and combined contamination of the toxic metals in commercial cat and dog food
2.citation: Du J, Zhou K, Jiang H, Hu S, Zhang W, Zheng Q, Zhou G, Zhang N. Scientific Reports. 2025;15:13237. Published 17 April 2025. doi:10.1038/s41598-025-98066-0.
2.summary: This survey tested 93 imported products produced in 2021–2022 and purchased in three Chinese cities: 45 cat foods and 48 dog foods. Atomic absorption and fluorescence assays measured five total metals. Chromium and arsenic were detected in every sample; detection frequencies differed for the others.
2.establishes: Cat-food lead and cadmium means were higher among positive samples. The hazard indices used maximum concentrations and human toxicological reference values because pet-specific values were unavailable; they are modeling results, not observed illness or species-specific risk thresholds.
2.relevance: The study supports measuring multiple metals, with detection limits and chemical species stated. Its cited Chinese limits are the authors’ regulatory comparison, not an independently verified current legal instrument. It does not establish a universal lower human-fish mercury limit.

3.referenceTitle: Pet food safety at risk? Investigating toxic metal contamination in Lebanon and the UAE
3.citation: Haydous F, Hassan HF, Shehab A, Alwan N, Serhan M, Dimassi H, Akoury E. RSC Advances. 2025;15:22629–22640. Published 2 July 2025. doi:10.1039/d5ra02790j.
3.summary: The authors screened 196 commercial products in Lebanon and the UAE in fall 2021, comprising 147 cat and 49 dog foods. ICP-MS measured nine elements. Table 6 reports mean cadmium of 0.251 mg/kg in cat food and 0.112 mg/kg in dog food.
3.establishes: These are product-group observations, not an ingredient-controlled experiment or clinical study. The study’s threshold comparisons combine disparate reference values and do not independently establish violations of binding pet-feed limits.
3.relevance: It supports regional surveillance and reporting product format and intended animal. Marine or organ ingredients as the cause of the cadmium difference remain a hypothesis. Human-meat maxima are comparators, not automatically applicable limits for compound pet foods.

4.referenceTitle: Evaluation of selected ultra-trace minerals in commercially available dry dog foods
4.citation: Kim HT, Loftus JP, Gagné JW, Rutzke MA, Glahn RP, Wakshlag JJ. Veterinary Medicine: Research and Reports. 2018;9:43–51. Published 26 June 2018. doi:10.2147/VMRR.S165890.
4.summary: The authors measured chromium, nickel, molybdenum, silica and aluminum in 49 maintenance dry dog foods bought around Ithaca, New York, using ICP-AES. Estimated intake per 1,000 kcal exceeded average human intake for aluminum, chromium and molybdenum.
4.establishes: Average human intake is not a toxicity threshold. The authors found no evidence of potential chronic toxic exposure under their extrapolated intake comparisons, while calling for bioavailability research and dog-specific allowances. This was not a feeding trial.
4.relevance: The paper supports examining additional elements and expressing exposure on a defined intake basis. It does not demonstrate harm from these foods or validate human concentration limits as optimal pet standards. Its 2018 description of missing standards is not a current legal survey.

5.referenceTitle: Chemical Composition and Palatability of Nutraceutical Dog Snacks
5.citation: Kępińska-Pacelik J, Biel W, Mizielińska M, Iwański R. Applied Sciences. 2023;13(5):2806. Published 22 February 2023. doi:10.3390/app13052806.
5.summary: This formulation experiment assessed four self-produced dog-snack prototypes, two extruded and two baked, including chemical composition and palatability. Table 5 reports cadmium, lead, chromium and nickel as not detected in all four snacks.
5.establishes: The experiment does not establish contamination prevalence in retail treats. Nondetection is bounded by analytical sensitivity and does not mean absolute absence; analyte-specific detection limits were not found in the reviewed methods. Palatability does not establish long-term health benefit.
5.relevance: The paper illustrates that treats can be included in analytical assessment, but directly contradicts the page’s claim that these finished snacks carried detected cadmium, lead, chromium and nickel. It offers no validation of a certification program.

6.referenceTitle: Directive 2002/32/EC on undesirable substances in animal feed
6.citation: European Parliament and Council. Directive 2002/32/EC of 7 May 2002 on undesirable substances in animal feed. OJ L 140, 30 May 2002, p. 10. Consolidated text dated 28 November 2019.
6.summary: Annex I sets maxima on a 12%-moisture basis: complete-feed lead 5 mg/kg; complete-pet-feed cadmium 2 mg/kg; total arsenic generally 2 mg/kg, but 10 mg/kg for specified marine-containing pet feeds. Compound feed for dogs and cats has a total-mercury maximum of 0.3 mg/kg.
6.establishes: The marine arsenic exception requires operators, on authority request, to demonstrate inorganic arsenic below 2 mg/kg. Articles 3–6 include general health protection, source investigation and a ban on dilution of noncompliant feed. Complementary-feed rules differ.
6.relevance: This establishes feed-specific comparators, not human-food legality or veterinary safety of every concentration below a maximum. The page’s universal 2 mg/kg pet-feed arsenic statement omits an exception relevant to fish and seaweed ingredients.

1.referenceTitle: Heavy Metal Tested & Certified (HMTc) Infant and Child Foods Program Manual
1.citation: Pendergrass, Karen. Heavy Metal Tested & Certified (HMTc) Infant and Child Foods Program Manual. 2026 edition, v0. The Paleo Foundation, 18 May 2026. doi:10.5281/zenodo.20270512. This is the cited first deposit; later editions supersede it.
1.summary: The manual describes HMTc’s product certification rules, including testing, status changes, remediation, mark use, appeals and disclosure of conflicts. It is the program operator’s primary account of the obligations and limits discussed throughout this primer.
1.establishes: It establishes what the cited edition says the program requires, rather than independently proving the program’s effectiveness. This May 2026 v0 deposit is superseded: its conditional permission for Status B mark use differs from the primer’s A-only description.
1.relevance: It is the main source for assessing the program described here, including the distinction between action levels and safety guarantees and the limits of remediation confidentiality. Version-specific rules should be checked against the current manual and executed agreement before relying on eligibility or obligations.

2.referenceTitle: The Counterproductive Consequences of Public Exposé Testing
2.citation: Pendergrass, Karen. Three Journal of Food Metallomics preprints: The Counterproductive Consequences of Public Exposé Testing: How Unstructured Disclosure Undermines Heavy Metal Contamination Reduction (8 April 2026), doi:10.5281/zenodo.19470572; The Cost of Operating Without Credible Third-Party Heavy-Metal Certification (7 March 2026), doi:10.5281/zenodo.18903738; and Certification as a Framework for Reducing Heavy Metal Exposure in Infant and Child Foods: Integrating Legal Defensibility, Scientific Rigor, and Commercial Viability (8 March 2026), doi:10.5281/zenodo.18905821.
2.summary: These three preprints by the program’s architect argue for structured testing and remediation, model potential business losses, and propose staged certification with repeated measurement and progressively tighter standards. They provide the conceptual background for the program described in this primer.
2.establishes: The papers present design arguments and illustrative scenarios, not independent trials measuring HMTc’s effect on exposure or litigation costs. Their deposit as preprints does not establish peer review or validate the current software that calculates program limits.
2.relevance: They explain the reasoning behind combining testing, improvement pathways and commercial incentives. They should be read alongside the manual: the framework preprint describes an earlier limit-setting approach and does not independently establish the primer’s later calculation method.

3.referenceTitle: General Requirements for the Competence of Testing and Calibration Laboratories
3.citation: International Organization for Standardization and International Electrotechnical Commission. ISO/IEC 17025:2017, General requirements for the competence of testing and calibration laboratories. Third edition, November 2017; confirmed in 2023.
3.summary: ISO/IEC 17025 sets a common benchmark for laboratory competence, impartiality and consistent operation. Accreditation bodies use the standard when assessing testing and calibration laboratories.
3.establishes: The standard concerns laboratory performance; it does not itself certify a food product or establish HMTc’s contaminant limits. The public ISO description confirms its purpose, but does not show whether any particular laboratory holds suitable accreditation.
3.relevance: It explains the laboratory competence requirement in HMTc’s testing lifecycle. Relevant accreditation and analytical methods still need checking for each laboratory; HMTc’s sampling schedule, certification statuses and chosen decision rule come from the program’s own requirements.

1.referenceTitle: Lead Astray? The Hidden Contaminants in the Australian Anabolic–Androgenic Steroid Market and Their Potential Health Impact
1.citation: Craven A, Ferris J, Nielsen S, Piatkowski T. Lead Astray? The Hidden Contaminants in Australian Anabolic–Androgenic Steroid Market and Their Potential Health Impact. Drug and Alcohol Review. 2025. doi:10.1111/dar.70007. Version of record, seven-page brief report.
1.summary: Researchers tested 28 anonymously donated anabolic-steroid products reportedly purchased in Australia during 2022–2024: 16 injectable oils, 10 oral products and two powders. Fifteen were mislabeled or missold; four of 21 with stated expected doses were within ±5%. ICP-OES testing found metals in all three product classes.
1.establishes: This small convenience sample establishes composition problems in the tested AAS products, not market-wide rates for peptides or SARMs. Metal concentration must be combined with product dose to estimate daily exposure; the study did not measure patient injury or manufacturing practices.
1.relevance: The survey motivates examining metal content in illicit AAS, but it does not compare certification policies, derive a universal non-detect target, or show that every detection represents a demonstrated clinical harm.

2.referenceTitle: ICH Q3D(R2) Guideline for Elemental Impurities
2.citation: International Council for Harmonisation. Guideline for Elemental Impurities Q3D(R2). Step 4, 2022; document history includes April 2022 corrections. Sections 2–6 and Appendix 2, Table A.2.1.
2.summary: Q3D provides permitted daily exposures and risk-based controls for specified finished drug products. Section 7 explicitly describes converting a daily exposure budget into a concentration using the maximum daily product intake, with assumptions and contributions from product components documented.
2.establishes: A concentration derived from a stated exposure model is a recognized assessment tool. Q3D supplies finite PDEs, not a universal non-detect requirement. Product intake, source contributions and analytical capability cannot be omitted merely by calling a result non-detect.
2.relevance: It supports HMTc’s use of route-specific toxicology while requiring the derivation and decision rule to be explicit. The source does not validate the page’s claim that every proposed analyte target necessarily falls below detection.

4.referenceTitle: Warnings on counterfeit and compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide
4.citation: US Food and Drug Administration. FDA Warns Consumers Not to Use Counterfeit Ozempic (semaglutide) Found in U.S. Drug Supply Chain, MedWatch bulletin, December 21, 2023; FDA Warns Patients and Health Care Professionals Not to Use Compounded Drugs from Fullerton Wellness, November 1, 2024. Current context: FDA’s Concerns with Unapproved GLP-1 Drugs Used for Weight Loss.
4.summary: The 2023 warning describes counterfeit Ozempic and needles found in the legitimate supply chain and seizure of thousands of units. The 2024 Fullerton warning concerns nonsterile compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide injections. These documents address distinct counterfeit and compounding failures.
4.establishes: They establish specific FDA enforcement and safety concerns, not measured heavy-metal contamination. Compounded products are not FDA-approved, but compounding has legal conditions and oversight; it is not synonymous with counterfeiting or with an absence of regulation.
4.relevance: These warnings demonstrate existing regulatory oversight and several safety attributes that a metal-only result cannot establish. They do not supply evidence that clear certificate wording eliminates endorsement effects or that the category lies beyond government authority.

5.referenceTitle: General Chapters <232> Elemental Impurities: Limits and <233> Elemental Impurities: Procedures
5.citation: United States Pharmacopeia. General Chapter <232>, Elemental Impurities—Limits, First Supplement to USP 40–NF 35 (official December 1, 2017); General Chapter <233>, Elemental Impurities—Procedures, Second Supplement to USP 38–NF 33; and USP Elemental Impurities Updates (updated January 17, 2023). Public historical texts and revision overview; current complete USP-NF text not accessed.
5.summary: Chapter 232 describes impurity limits and risk-based assurance of compliance in drug products, with exclusions and component-data options. Chapter 233 describes ICP-OES and ICP-MS procedures and validation criteria for alternatives. The reviewed public texts are historical editions; USP’s update page documents subsequent revisions.
5.establishes: The reviewed texts distinguish impurity limits, risk-based control and validated measurement. Chapter 233 allows ICP-OES, ICP-MS and validated alternatives; its quantitation criteria do not establish a single immutable instrument floor or prove that non-detect means zero contamination. Current full USP-NF text was not accessed.
5.relevance: They support documenting an analytical method and its capability. HMTc must separately specify reporting limits, matrices and the disposition of a detected result before a reader can reproduce its decision rule.
5.kind: Compendial standards — historical texts and overview

6.referenceTitle: Heavy Metal Index — peptides / SARMs / research-chemicals literature baseline
6.citation: Institute of Contaminant Standards. Research Chemicals, Peptides & SARMs (HMTc Category 26 master). Heavy Metal Index. Updated June 8, 2026; accessed September 15, 2026.
6.summary: The category page organizes a developing literature corpus across injectable peptides, oral SARMs, anabolic steroids and raw powders. It links primary studies and explicitly describes thin coverage and incomplete synthesis. It separates literature summaries from unpublished certification-threshold decisions.
6.establishes: This is an index and synthesis resource, not another experiment. Its author and operator are connected to the Institute of Contaminant Standards and HMTc; editorial separation does not establish independent institutional validation.
6.relevance: The index separates a developing literature corpus from certification decisions. It does not publish or independently verify the internal derivation claimed here, so it cannot supply the missing dose assumptions, reporting limits or evidence that certification prevents harm.

1.referenceTitle: USP General Chapter <2232>: Elemental Contaminants in Dietary Supplements
1.citation: United States Pharmacopeia. General Chapter <2232>, Elemental Contaminants in Dietary Supplements. USP–NF (2022); public publisher preview, doi:10.31003/USPNF_M5291_02_01.
1.summary: The public preview describes limits for finished supplement dosage forms labeled as conforming to USP or NF. Ingredient limits instead belong in individual monographs.
1.establishes: This review establishes the chapter’s identity and stated scope only. The subscription text, numerical exposure table, alleged adult assumptions, ten-gram option and claimed absence of other metals were not verified.
1.relevance: The briefing’s 500 µg/kg calculation is conditional on the unverified 5 µg/day and 10 g/day inputs. This preview cannot establish that the standard ignores children or that HMTc’s alternative protects them.

3.referenceTitle: ASEAN and Singapore health-supplement contaminant guidelines
3.citation: ASEAN. Guidelines on Limits of Contaminants for Health Supplements, version 2.0, adopted and endorsed June 2015. Singapore HSA. Health supplements overview, accessed September 15, 2026.
3.summary: Both sources give a lead limit of 10 ppm. ASEAN version 2.0 also lists arsenic 5, mercury 0.5 and cadmium 0.3 ppm, with a Philippines arsenic exception. HSA publishes the same general four-metal values.
3.establishes: HSA additionally requires safety for recommended use and target users, even when numerical limits are met. Its adult vitamin/mineral table is separate. The ASEAN PDF carries an information-only disclaimer pending finalization of its regulatory agreement; that historical disclaimer does not establish the agreement’s current status.
3.relevance: The lead comparison is supported. These texts do not establish that the limits are the world’s laxest, that all supplement regulation assumes adults, or that sharing adult products with children is prevalent or safe.

4.referenceTitle: Proposition 65 Safe Harbor Levels — Maximum Allowable Dose Levels
4.citation: California OEHHA. Proposition 65 safe-harbor table, lead MADL. California Health and Safety Code §25249.10(c), reproductive-toxicity exemption.
4.summary: OEHHA lists a lead MADL of 0.5 µg/day. The statute’s reproductive-toxicity exemption concerns exposure producing no observable effect at 1,000 times the exposure in question.
4.establishes: This is a daily-exposure safe harbor, not a food concentration or a general assurance of safety for children. The briefing’s phrase “observed-effect” misstates the statutory no-observable-effect criterion.
4.relevance: Comparisons with supplement concentrations require dose and frequency. The tenfold comparison to USP remains conditional on the full USP table, which this review did not access.

5.referenceTitle: Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 on maximum levels for certain contaminants in food
5.citation: European Commission. Regulation (EU) 2023/915, April 25, 2023; original act and consolidated text dated August 19, 2026, Annex I §§3.2.17 and 3.4.2.
5.summary: The 5 µg/kg cadmium limit applies to specified liquid formula made from cow-milk proteins or protein hydrolysates. The 10 µg/kg inorganic-arsenic limit applies to liquid formula. Powder and soy categories have different limits.
5.establishes: These values apply to specified products as marketed. They are not universal infant-food limits or supplement requirements; transferring a liquid-food value to powder or tablets changes the exposure basis. The consolidation is a documentation aid.
5.relevance: The law identifies the selected benchmarks but does not validate HMTc’s supplement limits, implementation or child-protection claim. Consumption and preparation assumptions remain necessary.

6.referenceTitle: Commission Regulation (EU) 2024/1987 amending (EU) 2023/915 as regards maximum levels of nickel in food
6.citation: European Commission. Regulation (EU) 2024/1987 of July 30, 2024 amending Regulation (EU) 2023/915 as regards maximum levels of nickel in certain foodstuffs. OJ L2024/1987, July 31, 2024.
6.summary: The amendment sets nickel maxima of 0.10 mg/kg for liquid formula, 0.25 for powder and 0.40 for soy-based powder, as placed on the market. The formula provisions apply from July 1, 2025.
6.establishes: The 100 µg/kg figure belongs to a liquid-formula category, not all supplements. Specified cereal provisions apply from July 1, 2026; lawfully marketed earlier food may remain until its durability or use-by date.
6.relevance: This supports the provenance of HMTc’s selected nickel number, but does not establish equivalent intake or safety when applied to a different product type.

7.referenceTitle: Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code, Standard 1.4.1 — Contaminants and Natural Toxicants
7.citation: FSANZ. Standard 1.4.1, instrument F2015L00408; related Schedule 19, September 13, 2024 compilation, §§S19–3–4; P1028 consequential amendment, F2024L01151, items 22–23.
7.summary: The dated Schedule 19 table gives formula lead 0.01 mg/kg and aluminium 0.5 mg/kg for specified formula, 1 for soy formula and 0.2 for preterm special-medical products. The amending instrument confirms the 0.01 lead entry.
7.establishes: These are category-specific limits with preparation/concentration rules. FSANZ describes the revised framework as Australia-only, with New Zealand opting out and a transition through September 13, 2029. The reviewed dated compilation is not a complete later-amendment audit.
7.relevance: The selected lead and aluminium numbers exist, but 500 µg/kg is not the lowest aluminium entry even within this table. Neither global uniqueness nor transferring these formula limits to every supplement is established.

8.referenceTitle: Update of the Risk Assessment of Nickel in Food and Drinking Water
8.citation: EFSA CONTAM Panel. Update of the risk assessment of nickel in food and drinking water. EFSA Journal. 2020;18(11):6268. doi:10.2903/j.efsa.2020.6268.
8.summary: EFSA derived a chronic tolerable daily intake of 13 µg nickel/kg body weight using rat post-implantation loss and a 100-fold uncertainty factor. High-percentile exposure exceeded it in many young population groups.
8.establishes: Mean exposure was generally below or near the TDI, with a small toddler survey around it. The briefing overstates this as general mean-exposure exceedance. The TDI concerns total intake, not a supplement concentration.
8.relevance: The opinion supports considering children’s body weight and nickel exposure. It does not show that a 100 µg/kg supplement limit ensures safety, or document routine sharing of supplement bottles.

1.referenceTitle: Baby Foods Are Tainted with Dangerous Levels of Arsenic, Lead, Cadmium, and Mercury
1.citation: U.S. House Committee on Oversight and Reform, Subcommittee on Economic and Consumer Policy. Staff report, 4 February 2021.
1.summary: Congressional staff reviewed manufacturers’ testing records and reported arsenic, lead, cadmium and mercury contamination in baby foods, alongside weaknesses in testing and internal company limits.
1.establishes: The report recommended finished-product testing, regulatory limits and public disclosure. It was an investigation of company records, not an independent testing study or an enacted safety standard.
1.relevance: It provides context for HMTc’s emphasis on finished-product verification and the familiar four-metal panel. Its scope does not establish that only those four elements warrant testing.

2.referenceTitle: Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 on maximum levels for certain contaminants in food
2.citation: European Commission. Regulation (EU) 2023/915, 25 April 2023. Original act, OJ L 119, 5 May 2023; Annex I, section 3.5.
2.summary: This regulation consolidates EU maximum contaminant levels for specified foods. Its metal provisions include inorganic tin in canned products, alongside lead, cadmium, arsenic and mercury.
2.establishes: The original act sets binding tin limits that distinguish general canned foods, beverages and specified infant foods. The applicable food category and exclusions matter; it is not a universal limit for all foods.
2.relevance: It provides a regulatory basis for including tin in HMTc’s coverage and matching limits to product and packaging. Applying a category’s limit elsewhere requires a separate, disclosed HMTc decision.

3.referenceTitle: Commission Regulation (EU) 2024/1987 amending Regulation (EU) 2023/915 as regards maximum levels of nickel in food
3.citation: European Commission. Regulation (EU) 2024/1987, 30 July 2024. Published 31 July 2024; Annex, section 3.6.
3.summary: This amendment introduces nickel maximum levels for specified foods in response to EFSA’s assessment of dietary exposure and health risks.
3.establishes: The legal limits distinguish food categories, including powdered formula, qualifying soy-isolate formula and liquid formula. Most apply from July 2025, with specified cereal provisions applying from July 2026.
3.relevance: This is the concentration-limit source behind the briefing’s inclusion of nickel and its formula distinctions. EFSA’s assessment in reference 7 explains the health rationale; this regulation supplies the food-specific legal requirements.

4.referenceTitle: Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code — Schedule 19, Maximum levels of contaminants and natural toxicants
4.citation: Food Standards Australia New Zealand. Schedule 19, compilation 6, 13 September 2024; infant-formula changes under Proposal P1028.
4.summary: Schedule 19 includes tin limits for canned foods and separate aluminium limits for infant-formula categories, extending food-contaminant controls beyond the conventional four metals.
4.establishes: The aluminium entries distinguish general, soy-based and specified preterm formula. The revised infant-formula rules apply in Australia with transition arrangements through September 2029; New Zealand opted out of those revisions.
4.relevance: These provisions support considering aluminium and tin in HMTc’s panel. Any use of the formula benchmark in another category must identify the jurisdiction, edition, preparation basis and rationale for that application.

5.referenceTitle: California Assembly Bill 899
5.citation: California Assembly Bill 899. Chapter 668, Statutes of 2023, approved 10 October 2023; Health and Safety Code sections 110962–110963.
5.summary: AB 899 requires covered baby-food manufacturers to test finished products for arsenic, cadmium, lead and mercury at least monthly, and to disclose product results publicly.
5.establishes: Testing began in January 2024 and public disclosure in January 2025. The law covers specified foods for children under two, excludes infant formula, and does not itself set numerical maximum metal concentrations.
5.relevance: It is a concrete example of a mandatory four-element disclosure panel. HMTc’s broader testing scope is a program decision; the law’s four-element list does not establish that other metals are irrelevant.

6.referenceTitle: Action Levels for Lead in Processed Food Intended for Babies and Young Children: Guidance for Industry
6.citation: U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Final guidance for industry, January 2025, issued 6 January 2025.
6.summary: FDA’s Closer to Zero guidance sets lead action levels for specified processed foods marketed for children under two, with different levels for different food categories.
6.establishes: These action levels inform FDA’s decisions about adulteration alongside other evidence. They are nonbinding recommendations, not universal safety thresholds; infant formula, beverages and snacks such as puffs are outside this guidance’s scope.
6.relevance: The guidance supports HMTc’s use of category-specific controls and careful identification of regulatory scope. It addresses lead in the named foods, rather than establishing a comprehensive metal-testing panel.

7.referenceTitle: Update of the Risk Assessment of Nickel in Food and Drinking Water
7.citation: EFSA CONTAM Panel. EFSA Journal 2020;18(11):6268, published 5 November 2020. DOI: 10.2903/j.efsa.2020.6268.
7.summary: EFSA reassessed dietary nickel using updated toxicology and food-occurrence data. It identified concerns for children with high exposure and for people already sensitized to nickel.
7.establishes: The chronic intake benchmark rests on reproductive effects in rats. High dietary exposure raised concern in young age groups, while acute oral exposure can provoke eczema in sensitized people. These are distinct health endpoints, not interchangeable thresholds.
7.relevance: This assessment provides the dietary-health rationale for including nickel in HMTc’s panel. The food concentration limits and formula distinctions discussed in the briefing come from the separate EU regulation in reference 3.

8.referenceTitle: IARC Monographs on the Identification of Carcinogenic Hazards to Humans
8.citation: International Agency for Research on Cancer. Monographs, volume 49 (1990) and volume 100C (2012); nickel chapter, volume 100C, pp. 169–218.
8.summary: IARC evaluates carcinogenic hazards using human, animal and mechanistic evidence. These volumes cover nickel compounds and other metals relevant to the briefing.
8.establishes: Nickel compounds are classified as carcinogenic to humans. The human evidence concerns lung and nasal cancers in occupationally exposed populations; the classification does not quantify cancer risk from eating nickel-containing foods.
8.relevance: The monographs provide hazard context for HMTc’s panel and show why chemical form and exposure route matter. Dietary nickel risk is addressed more directly by EFSA in reference 7; an IARC classification does not set a food limit.

9.referenceTitle: General Standard for Contaminants and Toxins in Food and Feed (CXS 193-1995), tin maximum levels
9.citation: Codex Alimentarius Commission (FAO/WHO). General Standard for Contaminants and Toxins in Food and Feed, CXS 193-1995, amended 2025; tin provisions.
9.summary: Codex’s general contaminant standard includes maximum tin levels for canned foods and canned beverages, with the two categories treated separately.
9.establishes: Tin is an established food-contaminant concern in international standards. These are commodity-specific Codex levels; they do not automatically become domestic law or apply to every food.
9.relevance: This supports HMTc’s inclusion of tin beyond the four-metal convention and its attention to packaging. HMTc must still compare applicable national requirements and select the correct product category when deriving a limit.

10.referenceTitle: Evaluation of Certain Food Additives and Contaminants (aluminium; tin)
10.citation: JECFA. Aluminium: 74th meeting, WHO TRS 966 (2011). Tin: 33rd meeting (1988), TRS 776 (1989); later clarification at the 64th meeting (2005), TRS 930 (2006).
10.summary: This reference combines separate assessments. Aluminium is evaluated through cumulative dietary intake; tin’s principal canned-food concern is acute gastrointestinal irritation.
10.establishes: The aluminium evaluation derives a provisional weekly intake benchmark. Later tin evaluations emphasize that irritation depends on the concentration and nature of tin in the product, and can occur around existing canned-product limits in some people.
10.relevance: These assessments support treating aluminium exposure and tin contamination differently within HMTc. They do not independently establish HMTc’s aluminium limits for other food categories, or make an elevated tin result a definitive diagnosis of can failure.

11.referenceTitle: Scientific Opinion: Safety of Aluminium from Dietary Intake
11.citation: EFSA AFC Panel. EFSA Journal 2008;6(7):754, pp. 1–34, published 15 July 2008. DOI: 10.2903/j.efsa.2008.754.
11.summary: EFSA assessed aluminium exposure from food, accounting for its persistence in the body and adverse effects observed in animal studies. Estimated dietary exposure could exceed its tolerable intake in part of the European population.
11.establishes: The opinion sets a health-based reference for total weekly dietary exposure. It addresses cumulative intake, rather than prescribing a maximum aluminium concentration for an individual food.
11.relevance: It explains why aluminium warrants attention in HMTc’s broader panel. Deriving an HMTc product limit still requires a separate rationale that connects exposure, food category and the chosen regulatory benchmark.

12.referenceTitle: IRIS Toxicological Review of Hexavalent Chromium [Cr(VI)]
12.citation: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. EPA/635/R-24/164Fa, August 2024; released 12 August 2024.
12.summary: EPA reviewed the cancer and noncancer effects of hexavalent chromium and concluded that it is likely to be carcinogenic to humans through oral exposure.
12.establishes: The assessment characterizes hazards and dose-response relationships specifically for Cr(VI). Its oral noncancer reference dose rests on small-intestine effects in mice; it is not a food concentration limit or an assessment of total chromium as one substance.
12.relevance: It supports distinguishing chromium species when HMTc interprets a total-chromium result. The choice of a screening trigger and the resulting certification decision remain HMTc program rules with their own justification.

13.referenceTitle: EFSA CONTAM Panel scientific opinions on lead, arsenic, mercury, and cadmium in food
13.summary: These five opinions assess dietary exposure and critical health effects for lead, inorganic arsenic, mercury species and cadmium. They are separate assessments with different endpoints and methods.
13.establishes: Lead and inorganic arsenic are assessed using benchmark reference points and exposure comparisons; mercury and cadmium have tolerable weekly intakes. Chemical form matters, particularly for arsenic and mercury.
13.relevance: The opinions support retaining the original four contaminants within HMTc’s broader panel and identifying relevant chemical species. They provide the scientific basis for concern, while HMTc separately defines its tiers, product limits and certification rules.

14.citation: NSF/ANSI 173-2025, Dietary Supplements. NSF / American National Standards Institute.
14.summary: NSF/ANSI 173 addresses dietary-supplement identity, declared composition and contaminants. NSF’s public certification description names lead, arsenic, cadmium, mercury and chromium(VI) among the toxic contaminants evaluated.
14.establishes: This is a documented supplement-certification comparator whose published screening scope extends beyond the familiar four metals. The public scope description identifies contaminants, rather than supplying the full standard’s numerical requirements.
14.relevance: It gives HMTc a specific basis for comparing the contaminants named by another program. Claims of unique or broader market coverage require a separate, current comparison of all relevant programs.

15.referenceTitle: ICH Q3D Guideline for Elemental Impurities; USP General Chapter <232>
15.citation: ICH Q3D(R2), adopted 26 April 2022. USP General Chapter <232>, Elemental Impurities—Limits; implementation FAQ, 27 March 2015 (chapter revision unspecified).
15.summary: ICH Q3D provides a risk-based framework and permitted daily exposures for elemental impurities in drug products. USP chapter <232> addresses elemental-impurity limits in that pharmaceutical context.
15.establishes: ICH’s table overlaps seven Big 8 element names and omits an aluminium exposure limit. Its default chromium assessment concerns Cr(III), with Cr(VI) requiring separate consideration; listed elements do not all require testing in every product.
15.relevance: The pharmaceutical framework offers a comparison of scope and exposure-based limits. Its element-name overlap is not equivalent to HMTc’s chemical-species coverage, food standards or testing requirements.

1.referenceTitle: Tampons as a source of exposure to metal(loid)s
1.citation: Shearston JA, Upson K, Gordon M, et al. Tampons as a source of exposure to metal(loid)s. Environment International. 2024;190:108849. doi:10.1016/j.envint.2024.108849.
1.summary: The researchers analyzed acid-digested portions of 30 tampons from 14 brands and 18 product lines. Among 60 subsamples, lead and cadmium were detected in every sample and arsenic in 57. Lead had a median of 173 ng/g and a maximum of 468 ng/g. Organic products had lower lead but higher arsenic; no category consistently had the lowest concentrations across metals.
1.establishes: The study establishes metal content in the sampled absorbent materials. It did not measure release during use, vaginal absorption, clinical effects, or inorganic arsenic and methylmercury separately.
1.relevance: It supports investigating contamination beyond organic labeling. HMTc’s certification panel, component sampling rules, and safety claims require additional justification beyond these occurrence measurements.

2.referenceTitle: Contaminants in Vaginal Tampons: A Systematic Literature Review
2.citation: International Consulting Associates, Inc. Contaminants in Vaginal Tampons: A Systematic Literature Review (SLR). Final report, version 5.0, December 5, 2024. Prepared for the US Food and Drug Administration, Center for Devices and Radiological Health.
2.summary: This FDA-commissioned review assessed nine articles covering contaminants, biomarkers, and health outcomes. It found limited, heterogeneous evidence, including the Shearston metal-content study. Small samples, self-reported use, and confounding limited interpretation. The evidence did not establish a metal-related health risk from tampon use.
2.establishes: The report distinguishes laboratory detection from tissue uptake and harm. It is a commissioned systematic review, not an independent replication of the tampon metal survey, and predates FDA’s 2026 laboratory research.
2.relevance: It helps define what a testing program can document and what remains a separate exposure assessment. Its December 2024 evidence window should be clear when used in an August 2026 briefing.

3.referenceTitle: Integrating experimental data and mechanistic modeling to assess potential lead exposure from tampon use
3.citation: Ellison CA, Doyle PR, Haven CA, McClenathan DM, Obringer CM, Woeller KE. Integrating experimental data and mechanistic modeling to assess potential lead exposure from tampon use. Toxicological Sciences. 2026;209(5):kfag052. doi:10.1093/toxsci/kfag052.
3.summary: This study combined lead partitioning experiments with a compartment model of release, menstrual-fluid binding, reabsorption by the tampon, and possible tissue uptake. Its four-hour scenario predicted less than 1 ng of uptake, under 0.3% of the modeled tampon lead content.
3.establishes: These are model estimates, not observed vaginal absorption. The calculation assumes complete lead release over four hours and uses a conservative permeability proxy from an intestinal cell model because lead-specific vaginal permeability data were unavailable. All authors disclosed employment by Procter & Gamble.
3.relevance: It illustrates why bulk content alone cannot determine exposure. It does not validate HMTc content limits or establish that tampon lead has been measured entering human tissue.

4.referenceTitle: The vagina as a route for systemic drug delivery
4.citation: Hussain A, Ahsan F. The vagina as a route for systemic drug delivery. Journal of Controlled Release. 2005;103(2):301–313. doi:10.1016/j.jconrel.2004.11.034.
4.summary: This review discusses vaginal delivery of medicines, including vascular supply, avoidance of hepatic first-pass metabolism, and formulation-dependent absorption. It also describes barriers to delivery, particularly for larger molecules, and the effects of physiology and the menstrual cycle.
4.establishes: The article supports the possibility of systemic delivery for suitable drugs. It is not a metal-absorption study and does not establish a universal permeability ranking among vaginal mucosa, oral mucosa, and skin.
4.relevance: It provides background for considering exposure route. Transferring drug-delivery observations to metal species or to a certification claim requires substance-specific evidence.

5.referenceTitle: 21 CFR Part 884 — Obstetrical and Gynecological Devices
5.citation: US Food and Drug Administration. 21 CFR Part 884, Obstetrical and Gynecological Devices, §§884.5400, 884.5425, 884.5435, 884.5460 and 884.5470. Official annual edition revised April 1, 2025; accompanied by FDA’s July 2026 regulatory overview.
5.summary: These provisions identify menstrual devices and assign regulatory classes. Cups and tampons are Class II; unscented menstrual pads are Class I. Some exemptions from premarket notification depend on product characteristics and the limitations in §884.9.
5.establishes: Classification determines the applicable regulatory framework; the cited classification sections do not specify a finished-product numerical metal ceiling. That does not remove material safety, manufacturing, labeling, or other applicable requirements.
5.relevance: HMTc’s proposed lot testing would operate alongside the relevant device obligations. Regulatory category and exemption status must be determined for each product rather than assumed from a single menstrual-products label.

6.referenceTitle: Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices (MDR)
6.citation: European Parliament and Council. Regulation (EU) 2017/745 of 5 April 2017 on medical devices. OJ L 117, 5 May 2017, pp.1–175. Articles 1–2, Annex I §10.4 and Annex XVI; original enacted text. Product-scope context: European Commission JRC, JRC134703 (2023), and Regulation (EU) 2023/988, Articles 50–52.
6.summary: The MDR applies according to a product’s intended medical purpose and specified scope extensions. Its safety requirements address released substances and certain hazardous constituents; Annex I includes a 0.1% weight threshold triggering justification for specified substances in specified devices. This is not a general table of trace-metal limits for all intimate products.
6.establishes: The regulation does not classify every menstrual product as a medical device. JRC’s 2023 assessment places ordinary menstrual cups under general product safety legislation; the General Product Safety Regulation replaced the earlier directive from December 13, 2024.
6.relevance: The EU legal basis for a menstrual-product certification claim must be established before applying device standards. HMTc’s monitoring requirements and adopted numerical values remain program decisions unless a specific applicable law supplies them.

7.referenceTitle: ISO 10993-1 — Biological evaluation of medical devices, Part 1
7.citation: International Organization for Standardization. ISO 10993-1:2025. Biological evaluation of medical devices — Part 1: Requirements and general principles for the evaluation of biological safety within a risk management process. Sixth edition, November 2025. Official scope and edition overview.
7.summary: ISO’s current overview presents a framework for evaluating biological safety over a device’s life cycle, taking account of materials, design, tissue contact, and duration of exposure. It connects evaluation to risk management rather than offering a universal pass/fail metal concentration table.
7.establishes: The public scope establishes the framework’s purpose. The complete paid standard was not accessed, so this drawer does not verify individual testing clauses or claim that every product must undergo an identical set of tests. The 2025 edition replaces the 2018 edition.
7.relevance: It supports distinguishing biological evaluation from HMTc’s proposed chemical surveillance. Compliance with a biological-evaluation framework alone does not independently validate HMTc’s metal panel or certification claims.
